maintopic: MEMORIAL TO CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-LAYING OF CORNERSTONE THIS DAY BY THE PRIME MINISTER

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, with the
unanimous consent of the house, which I hope I shall have, I should like to mention that at this very moment as we meet in this chamber this morning, another meeting is taking place in the town of Dieppe to lay the cornerstone of a memorial which the citizens of that town are erecting as an enduring tribute to the memory of Canada's armed forces who invaded those shores four years ago to-day.
At the invitation of the president of the government of France and the mayor of Dieppe, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) is being given the' honour of laying that cornerstone.

Dieppe-Memorial
I think it is fitting that we in this house should join in spirit the company assembled around the base of that memorial to recall one of the most gallant exploits in the annals of war.
May I be permitted to read into the records of our proceedings to-day four or five paragraphs of the speech which is being delivered there on behalf of the people of Canada by the Prime Minister.
After recalling that the men of Canada's army who landed at Dieppe that day, the men of Canada's navy who escorted them by sea, and the men of Canada's air force who covered the attack, were among the bravest of Canada's sons and that to a man they were prepared for any suffering, any sacrifice their task might demand, the Prime Minister goes on to say:
Dieppe four years ago was a momentary flash from liberty's revolving light. For an instant that light shore forth like some long awaited signal of hope. Almost as suddenly it vanished. For a while in the darkness of those fateful years it seemed to be totally extinguished. Then came the Dieppe of 1944.
To-day we see the Dieppe of 1942 as only time could reveal its true significance-a beacon light prophetic of victory. That light now shines in the fullness of its glory over the freed and free peoples of Europe.
Here in Dieppe on this anniversary we have in .mind the valorous deeds of all arms of the fighting services of all the free nations. But Dieppe has yet another significance for France and Canada and for the world. It marks a relationship between our two countries which is not without its message of hope to future generations. Three centuries and more ago brave and adventurous souls _ from Normandy sailed from this port of Dieppe across the uncharted Atlantic into the waters of the St. Lawrence. On its banks they helped to lay the foundations of settlement and government in the Canada discovered by the hardy mariners of France nearly a hundred years before. In the course of time the Canada of Cartier and Champlain was to witness the clash of rival arms led by Wolfe and Montcalm. But the country to which these Norman pioneers and their descendants contributed so greatly was to give another beacon light to the world. It was to give, as it gives to all nations to-day, the example of a people of different races, of different languages, and of different religious faiths, once at enmity with each other, now united as a single nation, rich in the^ blending of their separate cultures and cherishing above all else a common heritage of freedom.
In the first world war the people of France sarw the sons of Canada joined with their own sons and those of other liberty-loving nations fighting for freedom on European soil. In the war of liberation the world witnessed the armed forces of Canada and France again fighting side by side on the battlefields of Europe. In the mind of France to-day the Canada of Wolfe and Montcalm has become the Canada of Currie, McNaughton and Crerar.
It was not the men of Old France only who three and more centuries ago crossed the
Atlantic to face unknown perils and privations; nor in our day was it the men of Canada only who crossed to Europe to share the vicissitudes of war. The women of both our lauds, no less brave and venturesome, have played their role in the epic tale of early and present day relations between France and Canada. Many were the missions of mercy in which Sisters of the religious orders of France risked their lives in the days of early settlement in Canada. Centuries later nursing sisters in two world wars came from Canada to minister to the sick and the wounded on the battlefields of France and Flanders. What woman's part has been in all the services we know full well. This page of history has not passed unnoticed. In the hall of fame of the parliament buildings at Ottawa may be seen in marble relief a representation of the part women have played in the founding and restoring of nations. There one sees depicted the Sisters of Old France ministering to the needs and education of the children of Indian tribes in the wilds of North America. There also is depicted the service of nursing sisters of Canada in earing for the wounded on the battlefields of Europe. In the foreground, as the central feature of this relief, is a figure symbolical of humanity; in the background, wholly subdued is another figure symbolizing history. Beneath the memorial appear the words:
"To perpetuate a noble tradition in the relations of the Old World and the New, led by the spirit of humanity across the seas, woman by her tender ministrations to those in need has given to the world the example of an heroic service embracing three centuries of Canadian history."
It is the tradition of mutual service in the many relationships of nations that above all else Canada seeks to perpetuate in Paris to-day. The representatives of many nations are assembled in an effort to silence enmities bred of racial distrust and international strife. They have met to lay the foundations of a new and happier world. To this conference Canada brings as a beacon light of encouragement and hope the story and the example of her own national life. Canada seeks to see the rich rewards of international understanding, friendship and good will shared in ever fuller measure by the peoples of all nations. The people everywhere are praying to-day that those concerned with the making of peace may find it possible to lay well and truly the foundations of a better world.
This memorial will stand to future generations as a symbol of enduring friendship between France and Canada. Is it too much to hope that its foundation stone may also be a record of the country and the year in which the warring nations of our time had found a way out of conflict into eo-operation ? Whait could speak more eloquently of the wisdom of our day and generation? What more substantial hope of an enduring peace could be given to a war-weary world?

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MEMORIAL TO CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-LAYING OF CORNERSTONE THIS DAY BY THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the thanks of the Canadian people from one side of the nation to the other will go out to the citizens of Dieppe for the tribute they are at this moment paying to the Canadian forces, particularly the forces which attempted to
Dieppe-Memorial

find a way to get into the continent of Europe when it was so strongly held by the German forces. It was my privilege eighteen or twenty months ago to visit the site of that invasion. I remember very well walking through the streets of Dieppe, filled as they were with debris, and fenced off at nearly every comer by concrete barriers. I remember standing on the beaches and wondering how any man could come back alive after the fire that must have been showered upon them. I remember standing on the heights and looking down on those beaches where so many were killed. In the midst of that environment I could not help but think that only a miracle made it possible for any of the Canadian forces to come back from the inferno of that raid.
I wondered what it must have felt like to be a member of the Canadian force on that occasion; and it is a matter of regret that at this moment as I look behind me I do not find in his seat one who took part in that invasion and who as a result of his contribution was awarded the Victoria Cross. I am sorry that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) is not in his place.
One memory above all others that I carry with me from that visit to Dieppe was a story given to me by the people of that community. I have forgotten what the official called himself; he was in charge of the affairs of the city after the Germans had been driven out but before the war was over. I was told of the circumstances of that day in 1942 when our boys suffered such heavy casualties- over 3,000, including, if my memory serves me aright, some 700 dead. The story was that the Germans were about to bury our dead in a common grave, when, as I am sure all Canadian people will be glad to remember, the citizens of Dieppe, at that time in a defeated and occupied country, asked for the privilege of giving our boys an honoured burial each in a grave of his own. So they picked out a field for a cemetery on the gentle slope of a hillside two or three miles-perhaps more; I am speaking from memory-from Dieppe; and there, if you go to-day, you will see the graves of the honoured dead of the Canadian forces who fell in that assault. As I moved up and down among the white crosses I saw, as I had seen at other cemeteries in France where the name of the soldier was not known, these words on his cross, "Known unto God."
Mr. Speaker, I think it is peculiarly appropriate that we should be meeting in this house here in Canada when our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is laying the cornerstone of a memorial to our forces, a memorial erected

by the citizens of Dieppe. I think I can say with the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that Canada stands to-day where she stood before, for the right of each nation to determine the character of its own future. We are glad that, our men had a part in liberating France. We appreciate this expression on the part of the citizens of one section of France for the part our forces paid in liberating their country; and we trust that our relationship with that old land will continue to be what it has been for so many years-one of mutual trust and confidence and good will.

If the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the boys of the Mount Royal regiment and all the others who were there, it was not to make a sacrifiec; it was to beat the Hun. I am sick of hearing of sacrifice or that the soldier thinks of sacrifice at the moment of battle. They are not Isaacs going to the altar of sacrifice; they are men of flesh and blood who go there to defeat the enemy. I am sure that if they were asked what they were doing there they would say that they were doing a job. They were fighting so that there would be no more war. That was said of world war I, and it was repeated of world war II, but no progress has been made.
I sympathize with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who lost his son during the Dieppe raid. My heart is with him; he has the sympathy of all of us. But all that sympathy will not bring his son to life. It will not prevent his other son and the other Canadian boys from engaging in these wars which are decided by old men, men above military age who forget that God restrained the hand of Abraham when he was about to sacrifice Isaac. That is the history of the past, the history of the Old Testament, and it should not be forgotten in our time. We see these old men coming here making speeches, telling us of the sacrifices which we should not forget. That is true; I am all for praising these men, but something should be done so that history will not repeat itself a third time and the boys shall not be Sacrificed to the fire-eaters and the warmongers of Europe. This is a time when it is more important than ever to understand that the only way to do something in proper relation to the marvellous task which has been performed by our boys and by the boys of all the united nations, is to act in accordance with what they have done, to be practical and to put a stop to that warmongering spirit which has been the disaster of the world, so that it shall not rise again.

maintopic: MEMORIAL TO CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-LAYING OF CORNERSTONE THIS DAY BY THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MEMORIAL TO CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-LAYING OF CORNERSTONE THIS DAY BY THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the house for their ^ more than kind reception of me this morning, which I would like to accept on behalf of all those who took part in the raid. 
Had I realized that anything like this would happen I can assure you that I would have been upstairs in my office. Many things have been said about the difficulties and the peculiar circumstances which we faced at Dieppe, but I know that everybody who went there was delighted to go. Despite all that happened we all felt that what was done was worth doing, in that from the operation great lessons were learned. In remembering the large number of Canadians who fell at Dieppe I should say that in the opinion of one who was there, the sacrifice which they, and their relatives who remain, made through their deaths was one that was well worth while.

speechtext:
1.	Is there a ceiling for horseshoeing?
2.	If so, what is such ceiling?
3.	Is such ceiling uniform throughout the country?
4.	If not, what are the various ceilings for horseshoeing, and w'hy is each of them different?
5.	When were such ceilings established and modified, if such is the case, and what was the reason in each instance?
6.	When establishing these ceilings, did the -wartime prices and trade board take into account the increase in the cost of iron, steel and nails?
7.	What was the price of horseshoes and nails for horseshoeing in September, 1939, and what is the said price to-day?
8.	What is the ceiling for horseshoeing (a) in Toronto, and (b) in Riviere-du-Loup?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRICE CEILINGS-HORSESHOEING
speechtext:
1.	No.
2,	3 and 4. Answered by No. 1.
5 and 6. Ceilings on horseshoeing were established for individual operators at levels established by their charges during the basic period, September 15 to October 11, 1941. Such ceilings were established by the wartime prices and trade regulations, which became effective December 1, 1941. Maximum prices for new entrants after the basic period were established at levels comparable to other operators in the same area. Horseshoeing was suspended from price control effective July 8, 1946.
7.	The board has no information as to the prices of horseshoes and nails in September, 1939. Both horseshoes and nails have been subject to price control since December 1, 1941. The original basic period ceilings established by prices charged by the individual seller during the period September 15 to October 11, 1941, were adjusted upward on April 1. 1946, to reflect the increased cost of production of iron and steel, 10 per cent in the case of maximum prices of horse nails and $1.00 per hundred pounds at the manufacturers' level with corresponding amounts for subsequent sellers in the case of horseshoes.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not
know- what the wish of the committee would be with respect to the method of dealing with these estimates, but in past years when we have been considering them under the war appropriation it has been customary to
Supply-Naval Services

take the various main headings which are to be found on page 275 of the estimates such as civil salaries and wages, pay and allowances, travel, transportation and freight, and so forth. It seems to me that it would make for orderly discussion, if the committee approves, if we were to consider the naval service vote under these twelve or thirteen separate items, having the general discussion take place, as has been the case in the past, on the item for civil salaries and wages. But I am in the hands of the committee.
Is it the purpose of the minister to make what we have been accustomed to look forward to as an annual statement with regard to the position in which the Royal Canadian Navy to-day stands?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It had not been my intention to do that. I had thought that we might treat these estimates in the usual way in which the ordinary estimates are considered. I made a fairly complete statement last .session as to the naval position, and subsequently in a number of public addresses, press releases and the like I have indicated "the general character and size of the postwar navy, and my plan had been to proceed with these estimates in the ordinary way.

Then I would like to
'take a few minutes to make one or two general remarks as we have been accustomed to do in previous years.
Last year the minister described the then position of the navy with regard to strength, and gave figures as to what he believed the navy would arrive at in the course of the next year or two. He told us that the government's policy favoured an interim force for two years, at the end of which it might be possible for the government to develop a larger and longer policy. He gave the figures which he then had of an authorized strength *of 771 officers and 8,003 ratings. He stated that the actual strength at that time was 534 officers and 3,383 ratings. Then we had a return made the first of this year which increased these figures to 751 officers and 4,364 ratings. In the course of the discussion of these items I have no doubt that the minister will give us the latest figures. The figures he has given indicate that he has very nearly a sufficiency of officers, but there is a great lack of ratings, and I am given to understand that that lack is principally in what I might call the middle ranks. The recruiting is bringing in a certain number of boys, fresh recruits; there are chief petty officers, some of them of the permanent service, and some having received their training
[Mr. Abbott.1
and having developed themselves during the war years have come in through one of the reserve services. But between those two there is a considerable lack of able-bodied seamen and of those who have begun to specialize in their training courses.
The minister also indicated that new rates of pay and allowances would shortly be put forward, and they were subsequently, but they do not seem to have been of sufficient attraction to bring in the required number of recruits. The minister was looking forward to augmenting the ranks of the permanent service by those from the reserve forces who might desire to continue, at least for the two years, and also by those who had already gone back to civil life but might reconsider their position and return to the uniform. The minister will describe, I hope, what progress has been made in that direction. My information is that a certain number did follow that line but they did not remain in uniform again veiy long. They slipped out again for various reasons which the minister may be able to explain.
He also told us what he believed the Canadian navy would attain in the number of vessels in commission. There were to be two light cruisers, probably two light fleet carriers, ten to twelve destroyers and the necessary ancillary craft, and he hoped to have frigates in reserve. There again we should like to have the figures of the commissioned ships of to-day. If I am not mistaken they do not reach anything like that number, and probably cannot reach anything like that figure because of the shortage of ratings. We had quite an argument when the minister was discussing this last year on the figure which he gave of 10,000 officers and men, which he hoped would be sufficient to serve on the vessels described. I think it is more than evident to-day that he has not sufficient officers and men to take care of the work ashore as well as keeping these various vessels afloat.
The position of the Canadian navy is in essence just what it has been over the years. Its main duty is surely that of protecting the trade routes, the incoming and outgoing commerce on which Canada, being an export nation, so largely depends. She has that duty to perform on both coasts, and the minister will describe how nearly in his opinion government policy will provide for protecting those trade routes. During the war Canada's navy received a magnificent tribute from the allies because of the services which she rendered. From very small numbers at the beginning of the war she developed extremely rapidly and she provided the vessels necessary for the convoys, not only for convoying the

Supply-Naval Services
materials which were passing from Canada but taking care to a large extent of the convoys on the Atlantic, at first half way across and then two-thirds of the way, up to Iceland, across to Scandinavia; and after the United States came into the war, they being so short of vessels, Canadian naval vessels had to be used to take care of tankers in the Caribbean. Canada, then, starting from very small numbers, was able to creep up to very considerable numbers, and she carried out a magnificent work.
But we must never forget that, even though the world had a second dreadful lesson of unpreparedness for war, we and the allies were able to overcome that lack of preparedness only because of what a famous United States citizen described as "the phony war," and if war does hit us again we must truly believe that we shall not have any period in which we can slowly, carefully, methodically develop our forces; in other words we must be prepared. And what must we be prepared for? We must be prepared to provide such naval strength as will enable us to look after Canada's interests in whatever war may come. As in the past, so in the future: we can only think of doing that by collaboration with allies.
Next month, I believe, in London there will meet the heads of the services of the commonwealth defence forces. They will speak each for themselves and prepare plans in collaboration with each other for the part which each will be ready to play if war comes, and even in the years of peace during which preparation can be made. I do not know whether at this stage the minister will be prepared to give the committee any indication of the line of argument which our naval representatives will take at that conference.
Besides that, there is still in existence the joint defence committee of the United States and Canada, to which I think representatives of the United Kingdom come, at least in a consultative capacity. I hope the minister will indicate what the government's policy for the future is with regard to the Royal Canadian Navy, in that cooperation with the United Kingdom and the United States, because in those two navies, with which we must collaborate, there will be differences of training, equipment, weapons, munitions, and general conduct of naval affairs. I should be very much interested therefore in learning in which direction in those regards the Canadian navy is expected to lean. If she is going to collaborate principally with the United Kingdom navy, she will be so guided in her actions with regard to equipment and training and ammunition; but if on the other hand it is
expected that on the Atlantic and the Pacific she will principally collaborate with the United States navy, the answers to these questions will undoubtedly be different.
There is another matter on which I hope the minister will inform the committee with regard to his proposals for the future, and that is the great necessity, which exists more than ever after this second great war, to arrange that the navy and the air force shall be most cooperative. It is true that Canada has provided herself or is providing herself with two light fleet carriers. That goes some distance towards the cooperation which I seek. But in the manoeuvres which, small as they have been in the past, will I hope be very greatly increased in the future, both with the United Kingdom fleets and the United States fleets, there will be opportunities for a great deal more cooperation between navy and air than there has ever been yet. I should like the minister to describe the government's policy with regard to the training of' pilots for the air arm of the Canadian navy, and to give us the assurance that cooperative action between those two members of the defence forces is to be carried out with greater intensity in the future than in the past.
Further remarks I think I will leave until we reach the items; but I should like the minister to give us some understanding of what the actual position to-day is with the Canadian navy.

Before the minister
answers I would ask the hon. gentlemen who compose the committee to look at page 275, "Naval Services," and something will strike them: it is that "pay and allowances," meaning the pay and allowances of the crews of the ships, have been reduced from $98 million to $16 million. That means either that the crews of the ships will be six times less than they were during the war, or that there will be a considerable reduction of pay, that they will receive only one-sixth of what they had during the war-which would be an absurdity. I address my remarks through the Chair to the hon. member for Lake Centre, to my hon. friend from Skeena, whom I like and everybody likes very much; to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, to my genial friend the hon. member for Trinity, and all those who fight against bureaucracy; to the hon. member for Nanaimo, and to the hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard, whom we have hailed to-day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is this a new party you are building up?

I might make a suggestion on those lines. But no; I make a special
Supply-ATaval Services

appeal to all those in this chamber who complain about bureaucracy, that now the time has come to curb bureaucracy. I admire the sailors. I tried to have some accepted in the department, but always there are very high obstacles to cross before a French Canadian is admitted, and not in the department but on a ship, to get his training. All sorts of qualifications are required. It seems to me that the high officials of the department-I except the minister and the deputy minister, for whom I have great respect-do not want a single French Canadian to get on board the ships. That is my idea of it. We receive silly replies from these brass hats; they procrastinate.
Here is my case. Let us look together at page 275, "Naval Services." Last year the amount for pay and allowances was 898 million. This year it was reduced to $16 million, less than one-sixth, which means that there are fewer men on the ships. That is my first point. Yet, incredible though it seems, Mr. Chairman, the salaries of the brass hats are twice what the amount was last year. I expected the minister to announce some kind of reform, the curtailment of useless branches and sub-branches of the department, and what do we find? Civil salaries and wages have increased from $7,000,000 last year, when apparently the crews were six times as large, to $13,000,000, or nearly twice as much. How can anyone who will not denounce it, who will not oppose it, say a word against bureaucracy afterwards? Opinions are free, surely. But this is an encroachment, an enlargement of bureaucracy, and I denounce it bitterly because those who are in charge of the department down there, except the minister and his assistant, are procrastinating asses, and it is impossible to make them move. They are stupid, and it was in spite of them that the men in charge of the fleet made a success of the Canadian navy after Admiral Nelles had left. When Admiral N'elles was there he was a real man.
Here we are, listening to academic speeches about the work the navy has done. It is all right; I agree with that. I agree with all the praise given the navy-but the navy on ships, not the navy on H.M.C.S. Ottawa.
Bytown.

Yes, H.M.CB. Bytown.
This morning we honoured one of our colleagues, a hero of Dieppe, and I am glad also to give all praise to-day to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois), who did supremely well in the navy. If very feiw have heard about it, it is because of that hon. gentleman's exceptional modesty, but he served his country very well and he knows [Mr. Pouliot.J
his business. Besides that, he made personal sacrifices when he joined the navy to do what he accomplished on the high seas for the protection of the homeland during the war. History will tell, and I regret very much that history in this regard has not yet been written. The new members do not know it, but those who were here during the war remember very well how procrastinating the minister of naval services was at that time. His idea was that the first duty of the navy was to act as convoys, and that nothing had to be done for the protection of the homeland until the German U-boat came into the St. Lawrence river within a short distance of the city of Quebec. We had to urge him to protect our shores, and after repeated representations to him and repeated1 requests to the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet, we succeeded in getting some kind of protection for this country. But the country did not exist in the then minister's mind. All he thought of was to provide convoys. Hon. members will admit that I do not exaggerate when I say that. I was shocked when I heard him say so, but now he has gone. He was expressing the idea of some brass hats, Jbut I hope the opinion of the brass hats of the department of naval services will not prevail and that the minister will give them the good common sense reproach which they deserve.
What is the distinction one can make between a brass hat who had no military service, or someone sent here from England to direct the Canadian navy, and our own Canadians who can do just as well as brass hats who never had any service on the high seas? We have gallant men of our own, like the member for Gaspe, who is most unobtrusive and modest, and he has nothing to say about the policy of that department. I am anxious to see who will rise and protest against the bureaucratic requests for twice as much for civil service salaries as was paid last year. It is a scandal and I denounce it bitterly, It it twice as much, as will be seen at page 275. It is nonsensical to table civil salaries of this size, after the war, when the sailors receive six times less than last year.
For full employment.

I am against the encroachments of bureaucracy, and I wonder what support I shall receive. I have the support of one hon.

.Supply-Naval Services
gentleman from the west, and I thank him. I do not always agree with him, but everyone will admit that he has the courage of his convictions. Now I appeal to all hon. members, not only Liberals but all those who have a sense of democracy in their minds and hearts, to protest against it and join me in suggesting that the vote be reduced to an amount SI less than it was last year. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Before we go any further, perhaps I should reply to some specific points raised by hon. members. If not I am apt to lose track of them. The hon. member for Yale raised a number of points relating to the present strength of the navy regarding the number of ships on commission, and it might be well for me to dispose of that first. As at July 31 the actual strength of the navy was 8,216, made up as follows: Permanent force, 6,005; interim force personnel, that is those enlisted for the period up to September 30, 1947, 1,137; hostilities only, approximately 1,000; nurses 74. That makes the total I have mentioned. Since the first of the year recruiting has amounted in all to 2,631, made up of 1,430 new entries, 429 transferred to hostilities only personnel, reentries of 380, and enrolments of 392 from September, 1945, to January, 1946.
In terms of ships, as I have indicated during the past year, it is contemplated that when recruiting has been fully completed our strength will be two light fleet aircraft carriers, two six-inch gun cruisers, twelve destroyers, eighteen frigates and twelve escort minesweepers. At present there are in commission one aircraft carrier-the second, as the committee knows, is still under course of construction in the United Kingdom-one cruiser, two destroyers, one frigate and three algerines, that is aside from ancillary craft. When
recruiting has been completed the strength will be as I have indicated, with a certain proportion of the fleet always in reserve.
The hon. gentleman asked me to give some indication as to what the future policy will be. That I can give only in general terms. As I have said on a number of occasions, our plan is to have a relatively small but modem navy of ships of the most modern type capable of operating in close cooperation if need be with either the British navy or the navy of the United States.
As to whether our equipment will be of the type used in the British or United States navy, I can only say what the condition is at present. As the committee knows, our ships have been constructed largely in the United Kingdom, with the exception of the destroyers which are being constructed at Halifax, but they are British type destroyers. At the present time the equipment is British type. There is no indication that that will be changed in the near future, but that does not mean that the navy cannot operate in the closest possible cooperation and collaboration with United States navy. The policy will continue to be as it has been in the past, to endeavour to assure that the closest possible relations exist between our navy and that of the United Kingdom and our great ally to the south.
As to the matter of civil salaries and wages, referred to by the hon. member for Temis-couata, the position is that while there is an apparent increase from last year, from $7 million odd to $13 million odd, there is a very good explanation for that apparent increase, and I emphasize the word "apparent". It is not an actual increase in expenditure; it is simply a regrouping of figures which were shown under different headings in previous years. In previous years the practice was to show under the first item, that is, "civil salaries and wages", only the civil sendee position; in other words, positions coming under the Civil Service Act. The item of $7 million odd for last year included only the cost of those positions. I may say the estimated cost for the same item this year is $4,421,005, which is the figure which should really be compared with the figure of $7 million odd of last year. Added to that figure of $4 million odd for civil service positions is another figure of $8,622,801, which includes all other salaries and wages with the exception of wages of people engaged in ship repairs, to which I shall refer in a moment. The two amounts of $4,421,005 and $8,622,801 make up the total of $13,043,806 shown in the estimates. These miscellaneous salaries and wages of $8 million odd to which I have been referring, or equivalent items, have been included in every
Supply-Naval Services

year's estimates, but they were dispersed under a number of other headings, such as the fourth item in these estimates, operating expenses of properties, which included the salaries and wages of labour engaged in maintenance work; also the twelfth item, "miscellaneous stores and services" previously included the wages paid for all storekeeping labour, magazine workers, civil watchmen, truck drivers, boom defence workers, civil maids, waitresses, laundry workers, and the like. It was felt that the previous practice of segregating only civil service positions under the first heading was somewhat misleading to the committee, judging from the questions which have been asked on previous occasions. I repeat that the first item for this year includes all civil salaries and wages paid for naval work, with the exception of the amount estimated to be spent on wages to ship repair workers.
It is evident, I think, that in the transfer from war to peace we shall now carry on under civil labour a number of matters which in war time it was necessary to carry out with uniformed personnel. A great many jobs which in peace time should be civilian jobs had to be carried out in war time by men who were put in uniform not only to ensure that the necessary discipline could be applied, but also to ensure that these men could be moved from place to place. That is now no longer necessary, and it will be found that a good many men who during the war were uniformed personnel have now become civilians.
When we speak of the navy employing some 10,000 civilians, which was the figure roughly as of March 31, 1946, to look after 8,000 personnel in uniform, and that was the figure as at the end of June, it has to be remembered that a very large number of these civilians are engaged in the work of repairing and servicing naval ships and naval armament which do not come within the category of progress to which the hon. member for Temis-couata has referred. In a moment I shall give a breakdown showing how this portion of civilian jobs is made up. The navy dock yards at Halifax and Esquimalt constitute what are really two very large industrial plants, and they involve the investment of a great many millions of dollars. They provide practically all the mechanical facilities, except the dry dock, which are required to repair, refit and maintain not only the warships, but ships in time of peace. The employees of these establishments are not civil servants in the strict sense of the word, but they are civilians in the employ of the government, and that side of the navy is therefore a large industrial plant. As of the 31st
[Mr. Abbott .1
of March, the number of hourly paid tradesmen engaged on ship repairs was almost 3,000. It should be remembered that the navy has not only to operate-
