speechtext: Yes.

Will the minister subdivide
it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall do that in a moment-I do not know if I have it-if my hon. friend will allow me to complete this general statement on civil labour and civil salaries and wages.
It has to be remembered that the navy has not only to operate, maintain and service its ships and train its men, but it has to look after this industrial plant to which I have referred, to maintain its buildings and shore establishments. Perhaps I might give a breakdown of the civilians employed in the navy as at June 30, 1946. Civilians, that is tradesmen, engaged in the repair of ships and armament, 2,188; civilians engaged in the repair and maintenance of dockyards and depots, 644; civilians engaged in the naval magazines, 626; civilians engaged in stores depots, 1,579; civilians employed as guards, 492; civilians employed as firefighters, 199; civilians employed as crews in harbour craft and auxiliary vessels, 439; civilians engaged at the reserve divisions throughout Canada, 123; headquarters civil staff, that is here in Ottawa, 1,197.
What was that number last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The highest number was 1,702, as at July 31, 1945. I think the figure for last year would be in that neighbourhood, and to-day it is 1,197, down about 600.
Have any establishments in Ottawa been dispensed with since last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps I had better be clear as to just what my hon. friend means by "establishments".
I mean office branches.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps I might just complete this enumeration of numbers and then answer my hon. friend's question, and after that the question asked by the senior member for Halifax. Other clerical workers numbered 791; other hourly paid civilians engaged at small depots, boom defence works and so on, as cooks, timekeepers and so on, 994; and civilians at Newfoundland, 129, making the total of 9,401 as at June 30. In the three months intervening between March 31 and

Supply-Naval Services
June 30, civilian personnel strength was reduced by approximately 1,000, representing approximately a four per cent reduction per month.
Two questions were asked, the first by the senior member for Halifax, as to the division of these men between the two coasts. I shall see if I have that information here; if not I may have to give it a little later. Perhaps this will give a pretty fair idea. On June 30 the number of hourly rate employees at Halifax was 3,313 and at Esquimalt, 1,690. These include hourly rate people engaged in ship repairs. Then the hon. member for Temis-couata asked if any establishments had been discontinued. I do not know that it is possible to say to my hon. friend that any separate department at naval service headquarters has been discontinued, but there has been a steady and fairly rapid shrinkage in the total staff, and that is still continuing. Some of the purely wartime activities have been discontinued, but the broad framework of the organization is that which is needed in peace time as in war time: the intelligence branch, the operations branch, the armament branch and so on. I am just picking those names out of the air; actually I do not know that there are branches bearing these names, but branches or directorates of that kind would be needed at any headquarters, army, navy or air force.
But what wartime establishments have been discontinued, please, if any?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall look into that question and give the answer a little later.

'Last year the service estimates were presented to this house in an extraordinary piecemeal manner. We started off with one service, then switched to another, then came back to the first one, then switched to the second. Hon. members on this side of the house urged- that the minister give an over-all picture of our defence requirements and explain the relationship of the three services, one with the other. I should like to emphasize the fact that though there are three services and the personnel of those services wear different uniforms, they must be inspired by a common doctrine; and I do feel that this house, before giving consideration to the estimates of the separate services, should have the assurance that these estimates have been prepared in cooperation and1 not, as in days gone by, behind closed doors with one service competing against the other for the meagre funds which could be made available. Can we have the assurance that the estimates for the three services have been coordinated?
Then I should like to ask the minister to give some further information as to the fleet air arm in Canada, or whatever it is to be called. I should- like to know What aircraft .the personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy are to be equipped with, whether they are to be equipped with aircraft by naval service or by the R.C.A.F., because I see no item in the details here as to types of aircraft or as to funds being made available under the naval estimates for aicraft.
Then there is just one other matter I want to refer to, a matter raised by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I regret that the minister did not see fit to relieve a degree of anxiety which may be caused1 in the country by the remarks made by the hon. member, who intimated that the policy of the Royal Canadian Navy was being directed by a class of official to whom he referred as brass hats who had seen little or no service afloat. If that is a fact it is a most serious charge against the administration of the department of naval affairs, and I regret that the minister did not see fit, when replying to the hon. member for Temiscouata, to reply to that charge. I hope he will now relieve the country of any anxiety which may be brought about by that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps I had better do that at once. This, I think, just emphasizes the desirability of allowing me to answer various members one at a time. The hon. member for Yale spoke; then the hon. member for Temiscouata. It is very difficult for me to retain in my mind1 the points raised by four or five different members in sequence, and reply to them all. I want to try to do it. That is the only point I wish to make. And I have heard the hon. member for Temiscouata so often talking about brass hats.

It is high time someone
in this house pointed out that the permanent officials in the various service departments who have risen to the top of their profession have done so by hard work. The majority of them have risen from quite humble beginnings. I think I may be charged as having been a brass hat at one time, and I should have liked someone else to get up to speak on behalf of these senior officers. It is unbecoming for ministers of the crown to sit by and let these charges be made without any attempt to stand behind the senior permanent officials.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend
for the little lecture with respect to brass hats. I have been in the house four or five years, and in my experience I have had occasion to speak in their defence. If I remember
Supply-Naval Services

correctly, the hon. member made reference to brass hats at naval defence headquarters, and I intended-and I still intend-to take issue with him on that point. However, as I say, I thank my hon. friend for the little lecture he has read me.
As the hon. member for Temiscouata has made his annual attack upon brass hats in the navy, and I feel sure he will do so with respect to the army-
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
*-I suppose it is necessary for the minister to get up each year and answer these charges, seriatim, and I shall be glad to do that. So far as his remarks are concerned about the navy being directed by men who have had no sea service, that of course is all nonsense. The present head of the naval service is a distinguished sailor who has had a distinguished record, and a record which I do not think requires any elaborate defence before the House of Commons. This is a hardy perennial every year, when one has to speak about high ranking army, navy and air force officers, and I do not think the hon. member for Nanaimo would expect me to rush to their defence. I will say that we have a very efficient staff, in all three services, and they are men, so far as I can speak for the two departments with which I am concerned, in whom we have the utmost confidence.
I do not know whether any other point was raised, but perhaps I should refer to the future of the fleet air arm. Before doing so let me say that on previous occasions, both in the house and in public statements, I have announced the projected strength in the army and navy, and, broadly speaking, the general composition of the air force. That is not news, and it does not need to be stated again. The house knows it; the country knows it, and there is no change in that policy.
I do not know just how complete have been the details I have given with respect to the fleet air arm, and perhaps it might be appropriate to make a statement on it now. The present plan is for four first-line squadrons of aircraft, plus a fleet requirement unit squadron, and for shore facilities to be shared with the R.C.A.F. The naval air component is to consist of two light fleet carriers, as has been announced, one of which has already been acquired and manned, and is on her way to Montreal on a good-will tour.
In establishing the naval air arm, every effort has been made to avoid duplication of facilities which are already available in the

Royal Canadian Air Force. An agreement has been reached between the navy and the air force based on this essential premise, and naval squadrons have already been operating for some six weeks from the air force station at Dartmouth. Under this agreement the navy operate all aircraft normally operating over the sea which are carried seaward in His Majesty's Canadian ships. In addition they will operate a fleet requirement unit made up of shore-based non-operational aircraft of various types to meet fleet training requirements which could not economically be carried out by the air force. The air force operate all aircraft normally operating over the land and the sea which are normally based permanently on shore with the exception of the fleet requirement unit just mentioned. Further to this, the air force, through their existing organizations, have undertaken the procurement of aircraft and stores for the navy, and also are handling major repairs.
The naval air arm complement has been laid down and approved in principle by the cabinet at about eleven per cent of the total man-power of the navy, but it has been emphasized that the percentage of air strength may in the future have to be raised to perhaps twenty-five or thirty per cent of the over-all naval complement. At the present time we have one light fleet cruiser in full commission, H.M.C.S. Warrior, but a small percentage of the air complement of this ship are Royal Navy ratings, shortly to be replaced by Canadians.
The fleet requirements unit just mentioned is in the process of forming at Dartmouth. This unit, in common with some air force units, is suffering from lack of air mechanics. Two additional first-line squadrons will be formed early next year-we hope about the time the second earner is in commission.
In general it may be said that the air personnel situation is shaping satisfactorily. There has been no difficulty in obtaining volunteers for air crew. A number of naval pilots already flying are ex-R.C.A.F. men. The development of the air arm component is progressing satisfactorily, and it is intended to continue the closest cooperation with the R.C.A.F. as regards joint facilities and training.
In addition it is intended to make a close study of army support, and arrangements are already in hand for army liaison units to be placed in our ships. This of course is in line with what the hon. member for Nanaimo was saying a few minutes ago. The object at present of the air component is to study and equip themselves for any role which they may be called upon to play, including anti-sub-

Supply-Naval Services
marine warfare, air cover, convoy protection, ground support of the army, striking and interception forces, and the like.
With regard to the future of air personnel, it is the intention that officers who enter this arm shall be also trained as naval officers. They will occupy executive positions in Canadian ships in the intervals of their tours of flying duty so their opportunities to attain high executive command in the navy will be the same as those of an officer in any other branch. That, I think, is of great importance, because the normal combat flying time of an officer is limited; and I think it is therefore important that the men coming into the navy as naval flyers should have a full naval career open, to them, and that they should be not only flying officers as such but should also be fully trained to take command of naval vessels in the same way as any other naval officers would do.
What is the size of a naval air squadron?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have that information at three o'clock.
What types of aircraft are being flown?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Seafires and Fireflies, and there is a possibility we may get some other types of aircraft for training. That is now under discussion. They are the latest type of British aircraft.
Under what item will it be possible to discuss the general post-war policy? I share somewhat the confusion experienced by the hon. member for Nanaimo.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I said in my opening remarks-perhaps I did not make it clear-that our practice in the past has been to discuss general policy under this heading of salaries and wages. It is hoped that next year we may go back to a full civilian basis, but in the past we have had our general discussions under that item. I should be glad if the hon. member would follow that practice here. After finishing the item we will stick more or less closely to the particular item under consideration.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few remarks to make at the present time, and they are personal. The minister spoke before luncheon of my annual attack on the brass hats. I will tell him that it is not annual, it is not monthly, it is not weekly, it is not daily; it is a constant denunciation
of an absurd regime in which the irresponsible have control over the destinies of the nation. I will tell him, and he must take my word for it, that I am not any more impressed by jocular remarks than by insults of the kind I got the other day when I was called a nuisance, an attack which did not go any higher than the sole of my boot. The task I am performing now I hope will not be a task that I shall perform alone. I am most grateful to the hon. member who gave his support to the cause we are fighting for, and I hope we shall not be alone in trying to curb bureaucracy in the war departments as well as anywhere else. Some progress may be made; maybe not, but I will ask as a special favour from the other members who do not give their support to that cause, which is the cause of the people at large and of the taxpayers, at least not to denounce bureaucracy if they are ready to swallow it entirely. Let them keep their eloquence to themselves or act in accordance with their words.
I will tell the minister that confusion has been caused in the minds of the people by the mixing of the various employees in the department who are described as civilians precisely to prevent the Canadian people from seeing that there is no effective reduction taking place in the Ottawa staff of the naval service, any more than there is any important reduction of staff in the other war departments. Either the war is over or it is not. If the war is over, there are many, many men who have earned fat salaries and bonuses for themselves and their dependents during the war without risking their lives, not even their little finger, who must be told that the war is over. That news must be announced to them. The war is over and your usefulness has ceased. I wonder if the minister speaks to them with the genial smile that is his characteristic when he pilots his estimates through.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not always.
He should learn to frown.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He does.

And he should practice reform in his department. The country expects it. If there are departments where reforms should start right away, it is precisely the war departments.
I have a word to say to the hon. member for Nanaimo, and it is this. I ask him for a loaf and he gives me a stone. I have already praised him. I have the highest personal regard for him, but I hope that he will realize that just because he was once a brass hat, and probably a good one, he should not feel that he must protect and take under his wing
Supply-Naval Services

all the bad ones. For there are bad ones, and by bad ones I mean men who are getting fat stipends from the state and are doing nothing, sitting on swivel chairs here in Ottawa and being considered more important than a Canadian citizen who runs the risk of election and is here to do his duty and protect the rights of the taxpayers of this country. This cause is very important. It is the cause of reform, the same cause for which our forefathers fought a hundred years ago. There on the other side of the house I see a friend of mine who not long ago showed me a testimonial dating back nearly a century ago. His parents were in polities at the time. They were fighting precisely against bureaucracy, and they won their fight, and it is just as sure that we will win, even if it takes time, our fight for freedom, liberty and responsible government. I may be called wrong precisely because I take this matter seriously. If I do so, I do so as a Canadian citizen.
I realize the losses the navy has made. To-day we have paid homage to the heroes who landed at one of the most dangerous places on the European continent at that time. They were supported by the navy, and the navy has suffered losses. But I remember very well that when Great Britain offered us ships because, of what Canada had done during the war, Canada was unwilling to accept that gift. The government said that we should not accept those ships, that we must pay for them. We would not even accept gifts from Great Britain. What an idea!
The other day I was dumbfounded by the statement made in Paris that Canada expected nothing from the meeting of the united nations. I protest against that. It is not within the power of any nation to compensate us for the losses of life that we sustained, but there can be compensation for our losses in ships and other material. I believe that we must get something. If we do not get any material advantage from the united nations at least we should put our own house in order before teaching others to do so.

The minister said that there were 6,005 of the permanent force enrolled in the navy at the present time. I have here a press clipping dated April 15 last, which shows that at that time there were 5,200 in the regular navy. That means a change in four months of only 800, or at the rate of 200 a month. At that rate it would take two years to recruit 10,000 of all ranks. I should like to ask the minister what the recruiting plan is, and whether there is a campaign on foot, and if so, whether it is going to be stepped up. Just what practical steps are being taken to get men? Is the minister 
satisfied with the present rate of intake? If not, does he propose to take any more energetic steps to get recruits? At the same time would he tell us something about the recruiting of the reserve navy? This same press clipping says that the reserve establishments are to be recruited up to sixty-five per cent only. Will the minister explain how that sixty-five per cent is arrived at, and whether it is contemplated that later on it may be 100 per cent? Perhaps he would give a general statement of how the reserves establishment is getting along.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The figures I gave before lunch for the permanent navy as at July 31 were 6,005. Recruiting there has been proceeding at a satisfactory rate. The difficulty in the navy is the same, I know, as in the army and, I assume, in the air force; it is to get specialists, mechanics, engineroom ratings, and so on. But recruiting is proceeding satisfactorily and if as we complete the changeover from wrar to peace and more ships are put into commission more active steps are required to obtain recruits, those steps will be taken. My officers tell me that they are satisfied with the rate at which recruiting has been proceeding. They are being fairly selective in their choice of men. A lot of recruiting is being done through the divisions. That was the plan-that the divisions would be used as recruiting agencies. A certain amount of publicity material in the way of explanatory booklets, and, I think, posters, was prepared for use by the divisions, but there has not been what one might call an intensive recruiting campaign. It was felt that the time was not yet ripe for that. As I say, the recruiting is proceeding satisfactorily.
As to the reserve divisions, here again we are to some extent still in the reorganization phase. As the committee will appreciate, in some districts where we have good reserve divisions the quarters which are available are temporary, that is to say they are rented, as they are clubs or something of the sort which have been taken over. One very real problem we have to face at the moment is the provision of suitable permanent quarters. It is a problem which, I may say, is also faced by the army in. connection with armouries. Under existing conditions it is neither practicable nor desirable to proceed with any building campaign. So in some sections where we have keen reserve divisions we have a very real space problem. There is also the problem of changing over from a wartime to a peacetime command arrangement, getting suitable men who will take on the command of the divisions in peacetime. That, I understand,

Supply-Naval Services
too, is coming along nicely. There is the usual difficulty that in some cases men who spent several years on active service away from their homes are reluctant for the time being to take on the responsibility of directing a local unit. But we feel sure that a good many of them, after they have had a brief change and rest, will be only too glad to lend a hand there, and I think it is desirable, as in the case of the army, to try to have as many reserve officers as possible, who have had operational experience to take charge for a time of local reserve units.
As to the active list of the reserve part of the navy, the progress since recruiting started on April 15, which is when we renewed our recruiting campaign, has not been as promising as we should have liked. The strength as of July 31 was only 1,080. But as I say, with the divisions settling down from their job of demobilization, and with reserve training becoming active during the summer months, better results are anticipated, and I understand that several hundred applications are now on hand. The actual new entries are 254 officers and 208 men as at July 31; and the retired list as at August 1, 1946 on the reserve side is approximately 3,200 officers, in the Royal Canadian Navy permanent force, 123, and the Wrens, 231.
Does that apply to the reserve which the minister gave last year, 18,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is our objective. At the present time we have only 1,080, or maybe somewhat higher, of that projected strength.

How does the navy intend to dispose of the naval buildings in Prince Rupert? A rumour is going around that they are to be torn down, and the people are much concerned, because there are many semi-permanent or permanent buildings which would be useful for housing, or for factories, and so forth. Another question which has been bothering the city of Prince Rupert for some time, about which I have had correspondence \yith the minister, is this. When is Brigadier Walsh's report on the damage to the streets of Prince Rupert to be put in the hands of the city council? I think the question was last asked in May, and we were then told that it would come out some time in the future. Well, the future is going on and on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As to the first question, it is always difficult to arrange these discussions in strict order, but I think my hon. friend's question would more properly come under one of the later items.
Well, will the minister hold it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will take a note of his question. I may say that two of the buildings to which he refers are to be used for the naval division in Prince Rupert. Perhaps I had better deal with the question when the proper item comes up.

What is the attitude of the department towards men who at the beginning of the war joined the service for say seven years, have now served five and a half or six years, and are anxious to leave to go to universities and become rehabilitated? I know that there are a number of applications for release from the navy, and the attitude seems to be to retain them in the navy against their wish.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am familiar with some of these cases; they have come to my attention, of course. The period of enlistment was seven years, and they signed on as permanent force sailors for that period. They are highly trained, we need those men in the service, and the general rule is that unless there are strong compassionate grounds which would permit of the man being released from his contract, he should stay in the navy for the term of his enlistment. Unfortunately it is that very type of highly trained sailor that we need in this transition period when we are turning over from war to peace, because our permanent force navy was pretty small and we are having to recruit it up to a strength far greater than we had before, so we need these men. But my direct answer to my hon. friend's question is that each case is considered on its merits, and if there are strong compassionate grounds upon which it is felt that a man should be relieved of his contract, the application is granted.
It was not of compassionate grounds that I was speaking; it was in connection with going to university. That has not been considered by the government a compassionate ground?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is not considered as a ground, no.
The minister spoke of the navy being an active force of about 10,000 and a reserve force of about 18,000. Will he tell the committee on what basis the decision as to this strength was made?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
These figures were selected after the decision had been taken as to the size of our post-war navy in terms of ships, and the officers were asked to prepare a man-power programme for manning those ships, assuming
Supply-Naval Services

that so many were to be kept in commission at a given time, so many in reserve, so many for training, so many for shore establishments, and so on. The proposed establishments after being put forward were reviewed by the defence committee of the cabinet and ultimately approved by the cabinet. That is the basis on which that figure was selected. The same thing, I may say, applied to the other two services.

That is the reason I ask the question. If we are to build any military force in peace time it must be based on a survey of Canada's man-power. I do not think it should be based altogether on the number of ships we intend to man. We have twelve million people in this country. Every military force is supported by the industrial effort and the population behind it. Therefore if we want to build a good peacetime force, whether army, navy or air force, we must have in mind all the time the man-power potential in Canada, and we should so design the force that it shall be capable of expansion to the limits that the man-power in the country will permit. That is a factor to be considered as well as simply the ships they are to man. We must have in mind also the expansion and extension of the force to an economic unit. In the United States they found they had less than ten per cent of trained men in the American navy when they went into the war, and they found that was spreading the trained personnel far too thin. If the navy were again to expand to the 100,000 mark, perhaps an active force of ten per cent of its potential expansion, and a reserve force of 18 per cent of that potential, would be sufficient to man it properly and have a trained personnel to handle the ships and the administration of such a force. Can the minister tell me whether there is any department at naval headquarters under which combined planning takes place-combined operational planning with both the army and the air force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That would come under the chief of naval staff. The coordinating group, as my hon. friend knows, is the chief of staffs committee, which consists of the chiefs of staff of the three services, with their advisers, and which meets regularly.

If I might be so bold as to advise again, I suggest that this is the wrong level on which to start planning. It should begin right down in the roots of the service. In my small war service I was on coastal operations, and it took over two years, perhaps three years, in England before the air force properly combined with the navy in an attack which eventually negatived the German
(Mr. Abbott.]
submarine. Planning has to begin certainly at a lower level than the chiefs of staff if policies and training are to be coordinated and carried out with understanding by the junior ranks. M!ay I ask the minister what proportion of the naval department personnel is now engaged in caretaker functions for War Assets Corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can give that information a little later.
Do the naval service plan to use jet aircraft on their carriers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think the same principle will be followed there as in the air force. Aircraft carriers will be equipped with the latest type of aircraft suitable for that particular vessel. That is the ease at the present time. We have the latest type of aircraft flying for these carriers, a type which is manufactured in England. One cannot prophesy in these things. All one can say is that we will endeavour to have the latest and most up to date equipment. The trend seems to be towards jet aircraft on land, and no doubt in sea operations, and if that type is used in sea operations Canada will use them.
Does the naval department plan to continue Royal Roads as a cadet naval training establishment?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.
Is the history of the development of the Canadian navy being written?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

Does the naval department expect that Canada will ever develop industrial capacity to back our operational naval force without having to purchase machines, ships, equipment, scientific apparatus and technical supplies abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have never claimed the gift of prophecy. Canada has made very rapid industrial development over the past few years, and I feel that that development will continue. As far as being able to give an assurance to my hon. friend or anyone else is concerned, that we shall be in a position fully to back our navy without getting any type of equipment or material from elsewhere, I would hesitate to make that assertion now.
Can the minister give the committee an assurance that Canadian industrial firms are given an opportunity to tender on naval contracts for equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There is no question about that. Canadian industrial firms are furnishing large quantities of equipment for destroyers which are being built in Halifax, as my hon. friend knows.

Supply-Naval Services

Of the establishment of
10,000	in the permanent navy, how many are officers and how many are ratings? Also, of the 6,005 we have at the present time, how many are officers and how many ratings, particularly ratings below the rank of petty officer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I gave some of that information this morning.
But there was no breakdown below the total figure.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps that question had better stand and I can give the information later. Do I understand1 the hon. member wishes to have a breakdown as between officers and men in the authorized establishment of 10,000 and1 a breakdown of the present total figure of 8,000 in the navy, as between officers and men?
The actual breakdown of the 6,005 in the permanent navy and interim. The others do not enter into it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I can give the breakdown of strength as at May 31, 1946, of those actually serving, and I will get the other information later. Officers: 775 permanent force; interim force, 293; hostilities only 557; Wren officers, 43; nursing sisters, 67. That gives a total of 1,735. These will have been reduced since that day. I have not the latest figures. Other ranks: permanent force, 5,028; interim force, 1,172; hostilities only, 1,194; Wrens, 407; nursing sisters, nil, or a total of 7,801. The totals are: 5,803 permanent force; interim force, 1.465; hostilities only 1,751; Wrens 450; nursing sisters 67, a total of 9,536, which has since been reduced. I will get the others and put them' on later.
Mr. MclVOR: I should like to tell a brief story of the efficiency of somebody in the department of naval services. Last session the minister said that- if any boy was necessary to farm work be would be relieved at once or as soon as possible. Some days after that I interviewed officials of his department telling the story of a fanmer who needed his boy at home. Less than three days after the interview the boy was brought back home from the occupational forces in Germany and landed on the shores of Canada. Not all the work done by the Department of National Defence is blundering. To me that was efficient service, and it helped a farmer who otherwise would not have been able to put in his crop.

I should like to address a question to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. The question might appropriately be asked also on the estimates of the Department of National Defence, Army.
It has to do with the matter of demobilization. Unfortunately I have not before me the naval order which is involved. I am assured that a similar situation exists in the army. The question has to do with army routine order 2232 and appendix and some amending P.C.'s-the numbers of which I can give the minister if he requires them-and with members of the various services who were discharged from one branch of the service in order to serve in another. To my knowledge the interpretation which is being put on this routine order as amended by these seven various P.C.'s is that personnel serving in one branch of the service, in the army itself, the air force or the navy, on being discharged for the purpose of being commissioned or appointed to another, would not, according to the terms of the routine order, be given a discharge button for the service which they performed in the original branch to which they were attached. My information is that those in authority in both the army and the navy branches, which are under the minister, are interpreting the routine order to apply to those who were discharged in order to enlist in another branch of the service. But it has happened that some members who served creditably in the army or navy, and some for a considerable period of time, were selected for service in another arm for which they volunteered and for which they were adjudged fit, but for one reason or another they did not succeed in serving meritoriously in the branch of the service to which they went. A considerable number of these persons are now in the position of having meritorious service in the army or navy and have been discharged as a result of misconduct or their service no longer required in the navy, and they are unable to obtain anything to show that they did have a period of meritorious service. Is the minister aware of this condition, and will he look into it in both branches of the service in order that the situation may be rectified? May I point out that it has already been accepted in principle by the board which reviews the service of persons who were dishonourably discharged in order to see whether or not the benefits which Canada has awarded to those who served with merit should go to these other men. The practice is now that if a man has meritorious service in one branch of the service and is discharged and reenlisted or reappointed to another branch of the service from which he is dishonourably discharged and thereby deprived of these benefits, he does in fact receive them for that period of meritorious service which he had in the former branch. That being so I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that this consideration is being denied at
Supply-Naval Services

the present time to the men to whom I refer. I speak positively with respect to the army, and I am informed on reliable authority that the same applies to the navy. I should like to have the assurance of the minister that provision will be made for bringing the matter of service buttons on the same level as the benefits which are available for the period of meritorious service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall look into the whole question which has been raised by my hon. friend and make a statement a little later. I was not aware that action was being taken in the way he has indicated, but I shall give a statement in the course of these estimates or on the army estimates.

This morning a certain amount of discussion took place on the number of civilian employees in the naval branch of the department. I have two or three questions that I should like the minister to answer if he can. Are some of these people employed because the permanent navy is not up to full strength? If so, what numbers of these civilian employees are actually covering off jobs which would be carried on by the regular navy if it were up to strength?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can answer that very quickly. None of them are being employed to fill jobs which would be filled by the navy if it were up to strength.

If none of them are used for that purpose, are many of them used in demobilization activities which will presumably come to an end this year? What likelihood is there of a reduction in the number of civilian employees?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Quite a number have been used in connection with various demobilization activities, which, as my hon. friend points out, are being reduced all the time and which should be largely at an end by the end of this year. As he will appreciate, there is quite a good deal of work to be done in storing, classifying equipment, and that sort of thing, and after it has been done and the equipment has been turned over to War Assets we sometimes have to guard it for a time. It should be possible to effect a further considerable reduction in the number of employees. As I pointed out this morning, quite a few are employed in permanent activities in the dock yards and in the east and west coast naval magazines, the principal ones being at Renous, New Brunswick, and Kamloops, in British Columbia, and in things of that kind.

Will the minister tell us what the reduction is likely to be, approximately, when demobilization activities come
[Mr. Mutch.1
to an end? I was thinking particularly of one item which showed that 1,197 of these civilian employees are at naval headquarters. Probably it would be possible to get rid of a considerable number of these.

Hear, hear. I thank the hon. member for Calgary East. We are three noW; we are making progress. I appreciate what he has done, and I thank him on behalf of those who would have less to pay in taxes if we had not such an abnormal number of do-nothings in the department of naval services in Ottawa. I am no better informed now than I was this morning and at three o'clock, and it is now twenty minutes to four. I still expect a right and clear answer from the minister showing the reductions which have been made in each of the units or establishments or branches of the naval services department compared not with July but with September, the month which followed V-J day last year. We must know how the minister has been working to cut the ties of bureaucracy in the department; it is not a matter of expressing vague sentiments and cloudy ideas about the reductions which have been made. I want to have the information in black and white; I want to know how many of these do-nothings were in each branch last year and how many are there this year. The minister will not put in my head the thought that after both wars are over, the war against Germany and the war against Japan, the usefulness of all those in his department has not ceased. I do not cast aspersions on all, but naturally there must be some the minister can dispense with. I do not know the number of men who have been dropped from office since September of last year, and I should like to have a tabulation of those figures. It should be easily made up, if the personnel is as efficient as it has been described. This is for those engaged in civilian occupations, sitting in swivel chairs here in Ottawa.
With regard to the sailors, brave as they can be, let me tell the minister of an experience I had many years ago. I spent a Yule-tide at a dock yard, and I saw the number of servants the commanding officer had at his disposal. They were fine boys. One was shining silverware; another was shining brass; another was shining boots, and one could not interfere with the work of the other. One was cleaning silverware; another was cleaning china; another was cleaning the porcelain; one had the key to the wine cellar; another was serving wine; another was serving water and another was serving bread and butter. They were like the sands of the sea and the stars of the sky. I do not cast any aspersions on the navy, but I know the work being done

Supply-Naval Services
by those men. could have been done by a butler and a handyman; two men could have done that work very easily. But there was a cloud of servants, and we cannot say anything because they are in the navy. Well, even if it is done that way in England why should we follow that example here in Canada? It is time to stop those practices. It is unfortunate that they should be carried on when men are needed in agriculture, in the forests and everywhere else, when work is not done because we have not enough men at our disposal. There we have these men serving their country shining silverware, shining brass, the one shining the brass and not shining the silverware, another shining the boots without shining either the brass or the silverware. This is very important, and they take it very seriously. They take it for granted; that is the noble tradition.
Coming to that noble tradition, is there anything more foolish than that they should wear a black tie to mourn the death of Lord Nelson? Not only that; they wear the most absurd trousers, with seven creases to indicate the seven seas. Those uniforms are most uncomfortable; they are ridiculous, and they are not changed because it is the navy tradition to wear trousers symbolic of the seven seas and a black tie to mourn Lord Nelson.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why not?

Because we live in modern times. The Victory was a great ship, but it is tied to a wharf in the south of England. Does my hon. friend belong to another age, or does he live in the year 1946? I should like to see him in a sailor's uniform.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As a matter of fact I excel my hon. friend, because I have been in a sailor's uniform and he never has been.

That is true, but now my hon. friend could not wear the same uniform, which is very unfortunate. Here we are with the hon. gentleman who leads the house, who is most congenial, but who still mourns Lord Nelson. Let him mourn Lord Nelson.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why not?
Surely; let him mourn Lord Nelson as much as he likes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are proud of him.

Surely, we are all proud of him; he was a great man. I would not say a word to the contrary, but the sailors of the Canadian navy should do something else than mourn Nelson, and wear those long pants that are like bells.
They have done something else.

Yes, I know, and I do not deprecate what they have done. I admire them, but they are most uncomfortable. They complain about it, and when I speak like this I express the grievances of the sailors of this year 1946, the sailors who did so well during the war and who survived it. Somebody should improve their lot by at least making them comfortable. Perhaps there are many young men who would be ready to enlist in the navy but do not do so because they think they would look foolish in that uniform.
Mr. QUELCI1: You would not want them to wear kilts, would you?
No. I leave that to the hon. member for Winnipeg South.
Don't worry; I'll be back on that subject.

I leave to him the little petticoat which adorned him when he came into the house during the war, and I leave to him the other article mentioned by my hon. friend. But, sir, we are here for reform, and to reduce the number of idle men in this department, I suppose there must be some who will be idle, since there are some everywhere, but let us have as few as possible. And let us give the boys in the navy a chance to be comfortable when they go out, a chance to dress properly according to modern times and in accordance with modem uniform traditions of the nation. This is not a joke; I am talking seriously. I believe in the comfort of these men and the comfort of all those who are in government employ. The other day I asked for some improvement, I was not successful; I was told it was not desirable, but I still believe it is desirable to make men comfortable.
The minister is not a fanatic or a bigot; I hope he will change the policy of the department which now requires that no Canadian may apply for enlistment in the navy unless h,e is as learned as Pico della Mirandola. Why should a man need to have a university degree in order to be a sailor on a ship, or a stoker, or an assistant to serve meals?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He does not.

Some fine fellows whom I knew personally applied and were turned down because their education was one year short- of the standard required by the department; the minister knows that. Therefore I hope the navy will become modernized, not only with regard to the- guns on the ships but also in regard to the comfort of the crews, so that all ideas of bygone days may disappear and' the navy shall live in our time, in the year 1946.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

I am a little lost in the maze here. I gave some figures this morning on this item of civil salaries and wages, made up	to June 30,	which is about six	weeks orso	ago.	As the	committee will realize, these
estimates seem to be a kind of movable feast; you have to make fresh estimates every now and then, and it is a little difficult to know just what will be wanted. Speaking generally, however, our estimates for the year are based on the assumption that there will be a further reduction of at least one thousand civilian employees from the present figure. I hope and believe that the reduction will be substantially in excess of that, but these estimates were prepared some time ago, and obviously it is difficult to know just how rapidly the demobilization, both, of men and materials, can proceed, so it is necessary to make provision for the situation that may exist. However, I say now that our financial estimates are based upon a further reduction of at least one thousand, and I believe it will be greater than that. I think that answers the question of the hon. member for Calgary East, and I shall try to get a little later information for the hon. member for Temiscouata.
I was amused to hear the hon. member for Temiscouata, whom many of us consider one of the older traditionalists of the house, criticize the traditions of the navy.
Not at all.

I rise to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that in my constituency we have a well-organized and efficient sea cadets corps. They did excellent work in the last few years. The boys are being trained in navigation, seamanship and general administration connected with ships. The community has purchased a large headquarters, and has provided some cutters and other equipment. They have excellent opportunity for training because of their proximity to the Columbia river. I suggest to the minis-

ter that naval stores be made available to these corps, and that the naval department do everything possible to supply these sea cadets corps with available equipment such as small boats, navigating instruments, and life preservers. There are many small items which could be transported for the use of these sea cadets corps. What is the policy of the naval department in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I agree with what the hon. member has said about the sea cadets corps in his own district and the sea cadets movement generally. So far as equipment is concerned, the practice is to make modern up-to-date equipment available for sea cadets corps. The method is to issue it to the reserve division nearest the point where the cadets corps operates, and the division issues the supplies on loan as required. In other words it is decentralized to. the extent that the local division is given the responsibility of accounting for the equipment lent to the local corps, but naval headquarters determine how much should be provided. I can assure the hon. member it is the policy of the department to be as generous as possible in making suitable equipment available.

We had the same experience in my constituency with the sea cadets corps. We wanted to get a ship which would be suitable for training, because we are located right on the lake front, with a good harbour. The corps offered as much money as it could get together, but it was told that the amount collected was not sufficient to purchase the ship. It would seem to me the department should give some assistance to the sea cadets corps so that they could continue. I suggest the navy department give some consideration to this matter, so that suitable boats may be made available.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall look into the points raised by the hon. member. There is a generous provision, to the extent of $829,000, in this year's estimates for the sea cadets corps. As the committee knows, this is a joint enterprise. The sea cadets corps are under the auspices of public-spirited private citizens who give direction and guidance. The navy assists in the work of the corps by furnishing a finapcial appropriation to help with instructors, equipment and so on. However I shall look into the point the hon. member has raised.	_
What are the plans for the fleet air arm? Where does the minister intend to get recruits?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I discussed that matter at some length just before the luncheon adjourn-

ment. It was put on the record in some detail, so that if the hon. member will look at Hansard to-morrow he will find the statement there. If he does not find covered the point he has in mind, I hope he will ask a supplementary question.

I hope the minister
realizes that the questions I have been asking about these civilian employees have been in an attempt to get a reasonable explanation as to the apparent disparity between the amount of money being spent by the naval branch and that spent by the army and air force on civil salaries. I have suggested two possible reasons, one of which was that some of these men were being used to cover up vacancies which exist in the permanent naval ranks. The minister says that is not so. If it is not so, and if there is to be a reduction of perhaps only a thousand in the number of these men-and the minister hopes it will be greater-it must be that there is still a considerable disparity, even if we accept the figure of $4,424,000 for civil servants alone and $8 million odd for people who do not come under the civil service generally. The amount for civil salaries and wages in the air force, with a lot more men to begin with, is still $5 million odd and in the army, with a very much larger number, it is $7 million odd.

But they do not operate
dock yards.

navy there are a considerable number of establishments of one kind or another partly operated with civilian help, and I suggest that offsets this dock yard element. Is there any other reason for this apparent disparity?
[DOT]-because there certainly is a disparity of some considerable amount.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I suggest that if my hon.
friend analyses other estimates he will find that there are some civil salaries and wages carried in the army estimates, for instance, under other headings. We have attempted this year in connection with the navy to bring them under this one item. As I said this morning, that differs from the practice in previous years. I agree with everything said by the hon. member, or by any other hon. member, that it is desirable to cut down the number of civilian employees. Let me assure the committee that I am driving at that every day. I realize that the proportion appears high, although I am not prepared to say it is too high. Indeed I do not think it is, to-day. I am told that in the navy, by reason of the operation of dock
yards, and some other activities, the ratio of civilian employees is higher than in the other two services. I am advised that that is true in the case of the admiralty, although I have no personal knowledge of that.
I am glad this matter has been brought up, because it will second my own efforts to cut down the number of civilian employees to the lowest possible number consistent with the maintenance of a strong and efficient navy.
I take no exception to the criticism of the ' hon. member respecting civilian employees, but I am only doing my best to explain why there are these numbers. I assure the committee I am doing my best to see that they are kept within proper proportions.

I thoroughly agree with the minister that all civilian employees should be listed under one heading so far as civil salaries and wages are concerned. He has indicated that that is being done for the navy. If it has not been done in the army and air force estimates I would request that civilian salaries under those departments be brought in under a separate heading, so that we may have a better opportunity to make comparisons and to know to what extent civilian salaries and wages are being paid in those two services. ,
Going back to the matter of recruiting, on what date does the minister say that the 10,000 men will be enlisted?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
We rather hoped that we would be close to that objective by about the end of the present fiscal year. The staff tell me that that would suit their plans very well in arranging the manning of various ships and changing over from war to peace. It will certainly not be earlier than the end of the present fiscal year, and probably not until a bit later. To be more specific, we hope to have something around 8,700 by the end of this current fiscal year, March 31. Our second carrier will not be in commission, we expect-, until some time next year. That of course has a direct relationship to the number of permanent force personnel we wish to take into the Service. She carries a complement of about 1,000 men.
.Mr. MERRITT: In February the minister was quoted as saying that one carrier and four destroyers will probably have to be carried in reserve because of the 10,000-men limit. So from the figures he gave this morning it appears there are very few destroyers in commission-only two out of twelve-and one
Supply-Naval Services

frigate out of eighteen. Therefore it would seem to me that the 10,000 objective will not be much affected by the carrier.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We cannot just leave her standing idle. Even in reserve she carries men.
I understand that, but not a full complement.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.

At the present rate of recruiting, 200 a month, it will take twenty-five months to reach 10,000. If we are going to have 10,000 in this fiscal year, as there are only about six months left the rate will have to be quadrupled and you will have to take in about 800 a month. I throw out this suggestion. As an extra aid in recruiting I cannot think of anything better than that the minister himself should go out and speak in some of the principal cities in Canada and encourage young Canadians to join the service. With such encouragement I am sure that a large number would come forward. The minister can be the best recruiting agency we could possibly have, and probably he will cost less than others.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I sincerely thank my hon. friend for his very generous tribute to my oratorical and persuasive powers. Nothing would please me better than to do the sort of thing he suggests, but he will appreciate that for the last four or five months it has not been easy for me or for any minister to get away from Ottawa. I hope that the session will soon be concluded-and while I am frank to say that I do not intend to go on any recruiting tour immediately after the session is over, I appreciate the suggestion my hon. friend has made. I was hoping long before this to make at least a trip to each of the two coasts and see our establishments there. I have done it only in a quick sort of way, spending a day or two only in each place-not from any lack of desire on my part, but solely because of more pressing duties at Ottawa.
I did not offer the suggestion lightly, and I hope the minister will not only visit the establishments but speak publicly in aid of recruiting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sincere when I say I appreciate my hon. friend's suggestion.

Quite a number of Canadians are now serving in the British fleet air arm, continuing their training over there perhaps more extensively since the war is over. Is it part of the minister's programme to bring these young men back to serve in our own fleet air arm?
(Mr. Merritt.]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We have a very considerable number who served with the British fleet air arm during the war. It would' not be possible to take all of them, because there were a larger number of them than our complement wmuld permit, but that is the source from which we have been drawing most of our flying personnel.

The minister in reply to the hon. member for Trinity stated that the liaison or cooperation between the three services was on the chief of staff level. I want to make a comment on that. It is the practice now in the United States and in the United Kingdom forces that every officer who attains command must have a knowledge, and in the United States a very extensive knowledge, of the functions and limitations of the other two branches of the service. While the navy in the United States has not a separate air force, nevertheless the liaison is at a much lower level than chief of staff, and I suggest that the minister consider seriously establishing a joint staff college so that every officer at the commander level or the squadron leader level, or even lower, may have the opportunity to understand the operations and limitations of the other two services. It is obvious that as war becomes more and more scientific and the velocity of projectiles much greater, a knowledge of the operations and limitations of weapons, and a knowledge even of the outlook of the other services, is very important for any officer in command to have in any future war. I think every one of them should have that. At the chief of staff level you find officers who are very jealous of their prerogatives, and the cooperation is apt to be on the surface rather than genuine. A man on the chief staff level is inclined to take the view: That is all very well, but I am running the navy. The same attitude will no doubt be found in the other services at the chief of staff level. But if all officers who are likely to take command had a knowledge of the functions and limitations of the other two services, I believe you would have a much more effective and efficient defence service. I suggest that to the minister. I do not know what plans have been made in that regard. I merely heard his reply to the hon. member for Trinity.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for his suggestion, and I can assure him that thinking along those lines, and probably something more than thinking, will develop in the not very distant future. We have an army staff college at Kingston which representatives of the other two services attend; also an army training station at Carberry and an operation school at Courtenay, British Columbia. On

Supply-National Defence
both coasts the air force and the army are cooperating closely with the navy. Anyone who has seen' any thing of war realizes that no army in the future is ever going to fight without an air force in close liaison.
And no navy in the future will fight without an air force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Right, and under certain conditions no army will fight without a navy. I agree that there should be the closest possible liaison between the three, branches of the sendee, and that is what we are endeavouring to achieve. I mentioned the chiefs of staff committee, but that liaison is carried on at all levels. The director of plans for the navy is constantly in touch with his opposite number in the other two services. The personnel members committee meets regularly to discuss personnel problems. The research and development branch, as the committee knows, is headed by Doctor Solandt, who was formerly Colonel Solandt. That branch coordinates research development for the three services. So we are making real headway in attaining good liaison between the three services.
I think every junior officer should know the functions and limitations of the other two services.

The estimates of the Minister of National Defence for the current fiscal year include, according to this document before us, $104,793.40 on ordinary account and some $488,608,641 on demobilization and reconversion account, roughly a half billion dollar requisition, and, compared with estimates we have been talking about before, roughly 200 per cent of our federal expenditure on health and welfare. This estimate is doubtless considered necessary by the Minister of National Defence to implement the financial outlay implied in the resolution, which has been standing on the order paper now for some months, which reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Militia Act whereby provision will be made for a permanent force of officers and men in number as may be authorized by 'the governor in council, and for the employment during the period of demobilization of such members of the military forces as may be deemed necessary for the orderly carrying out of such demobilization.
In connection with this expenditure I wish to remind the committee of a resolution presented to parliament by the minister of defence in the government of 1910. In that resolution the minister of the day sought to provide for a permanent force not exceeding
10,000.	That number was a 100 per cent increase over the force authorized prior to world war I. The argument of the then minister of defence in support of his resolution was that the internal unrest in Canadian

labour-the Winnipeg strike was in progress at that time-as well as the defence of Canada against foreign aggression, necessitated that increase from 5,000 to 10,000 in the personnel of the permanent force.
The estimates of the Minister of Justice this session showed an increase in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police requirements of nearly $4,000,000, or fifty per cent over last year, a total amount equal to roughly the full permanent force requests following the first world war. I presume therefore that the Minister of Justice has judged that his department is now properly equipped to attend to the peace, order and good government within Canada's borders, so we may conclude that after the demobilization expenditures of the Minister of National Defence have been paid, the balance of the half billion dollars for which he is asking will go to the maintenance of Canada's post-war navy, army and air force.
From the facts I have stated, it must be most evident that the government of Canada has somehow committed its people to an extremely large peacetime expansion of armament from the custom of the past. One third roughly of all the money to be voted by parliament this session goes to the Minister of National Defence for expenditure in the second year of peace. The permanent force is not limited in number, as it was in 1919, but permission is being sought by the minister this session to create a force in numbers as may be authorized by the governor in council. Such a procedure is contrary to all peacetime precedent.
Many of the most bitter conflicts between the people and their king in English history dealt with the peacetime maintenance by the king of a standing army. The Bill of Rights of 1688 contained this clause:
That the raising of a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, unless it be with the consent of parliament, is against the law.
Civil war has been waged in England over this principle in past centuries and now the Minister of National Defence in effect asks for a blank cheque on which he will place his own figures. With this power of the minister I must disagree, as did the citizens of England disagree with Charles I and James II.
The story of frontier America portrays an evolution in the maintenance of law and order that I feel I must recall to the house. In the unorganized frontier areas, each citizen by his own strength, and acting on his own concept of law or of right, protected his domain or pillaged his neighbour. Individual strength was the law. From the confusion of this system, in which might was right, a delegation of

Supply-National Defence
law enforcement powers was made, after considerable trial and error, properly to empower delegates of the community as a whole. The individual was protected in his lawful aspirations by the combined strength of the community, and under this system the strong and the weak, neighbour and stranger, lived in a security that was lacking when each man was his own sheriff.
A similar evolution is in making in the world community. The feudal barons who protected or pillaged their dependents and neighbours, have yielded their powers in the common good to a national authority. National military leaders in past conflicts have for the duration of the war accepted assigned military tasks from a supreme commander selected for his qualities proper to the occasion. In peace time the same delegation to an international authority must be made by national bodies; for it has long been self-evident that no single national state can defend itself against an aggressor, nor can a single aggressor state successfully strive against the combined forces of defending allies. Darius, Napoleon, Wilhelm II, Hitler, have all failed to disprove this thesis. The professional general does not defeat the citizen army. The volunteer strength of Canada's civilian turned soldier has matched Wehrmaeht in the past and is quite capable of doing so again should the necessity ever once more arise.
All arguments for the maintenance of a permanent peacetime force are invariably based on the need for preparedness against some foreign attack. To use such an argument on behalf of any peacetime force, that this country is able and prepared to equip and maintain for action against any possible aggressor nation, is ridiculous. Modern methods of warfare would make the defence of Canada, with its huge land areas and small prepared forces, an impossibility, and this I am certain that no exponent of military strategy could1 safely contradict.
Why then is the Minister of National Defence asking the house for an appropriation for such a peacetime military force? The Canadian people have no interest in becoming an aggressor nation. By ourselves we cannot repel an aggressor. The duty of the Canadian parliament to organize modern armed forces arises not only or even mainly out of our defence needs but out of our obligations as a member of the world community, pledged to help the maintenance of peace. In the Atlantic charter the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the President of the United States held out to all the people of the world the hope of four freedoms based on a world organization for the maintenance of peace and 63260-317
of security. This world organization, the united nations organization, is struggling to achieve that which its predecessor the league of nations failed to do. In its aim to secure international security it already has many powerful unfriendly critics. Not the least vocal of these critics are the proponents of nationalism and national armaments. The C.C.F. party feels that Canada must play a positive part in making the united nations organization the effective instrument for which it was designed.
At the opening of the San Francisco conference last year, President Truman said:
This conference will devote its energies and its labours exclusively to the single problem of setting up the essential organization to keep the peace.	.
The charter of the united nations, drawn up at that time and concurred in by Canada, states, in article 43:
(1)	All members of the united nations, in order to contribute to the maintenauce of international peace and security, undertake to make available to the security council on its call and in accordance with a special agreement or agreements armed forces, assistance and facilities including the rights of passage necessary for the purpose of maintaining international peace and security.
(2)	Such agreement or agreements shall govern the number and the types of forces, their degree of readiness and general location, and the nature of the facilities and assistance to be provided.
(3)	The agreement or agreements shall be negotiated as soon as possible on the initiative of the security council. They shall be concluded between the security council and the members, or between the security council and groups of members, and shall be subject to ratification by the signatory states in accordance with their constitutional processes.
While no indication has been given to the members of this House of Commons as to agreements, as mentioned in article 43 of the united nations charter from which I have just quoted, respecting Canada's role in an international protective plan, and while no such agreements have as yet been presented to this house for ratification, the C.C.F. members of the house are prepared to support a negotiated contribution by Canada to such a protective force, and are prepared conditionally to approve the mustering of suitable armed components in anticipation of such agreements being secured and ratified by the House of Commons.
The conditions which the members of the C.C.F. group feel should be assured to support such an interim set-up are as follows:
1.	That the number of officers and men be set, not by governor in council but by the parliament of Canada.
