2.	That the Canadian force be recruited on a volunteer career basis with candidates accepted on an aptitude basis only.
3.	That the terms of service be such that promotion will be based upon general personal ability, or upon special ability in scientific military research; that upgrading of personnel in military science and technical research be continuous for all ranks throughout the entire period of service, with syllabi drawn up to include studies in history, economics and world citizenship, as well as technical studies solely applicable to the service.
- 4. That the present undemocratic forms of drill and discipline be reorganized in favour of rational treatment of all ranks.
5.	That pay scales of pay and allowances, amenities while in service and1 pension privileges on discharge be more nearly equalized for all ranks than is the case at present.
6.	That the basis for admission to, and study in, all military institutions be individual ability only, without regard to race, creed or colour; that the curriculi of these institutions be based on modern social and military needs, to include the historic study of the causes and results of war, and that all permanent force personnel be automatically eligible for admission.
7.	That all scientific discoveries of the Canadian force or of military research laboratories be made available to the united nations assembly on a reciprocal basis, and where research results have humanitarian value, that the findings be passed on for the general benefit.
8.	That army, navy and air force be integrated into a unified group for combined operations under a single staff, under direction of and through continuous liaison with the united nations protective force as required and when established.
9.	That non-technical staff (of high ranking officers) be drastically reduced and senior staff officers regularly reexamined and retired from the service to make way for younger and more efficient officers.
10.	That the present military districts headquarters staffs be retired on discharge of active army, and that the complements of area staffs and national defence headquarters staff be reduced to such number and with such functions as to maintain efficient military requirements.
11.	That all activities of and appropriations for the Canadian armed forces be subject to continuous review and control by a standing committee of the House of Commons. In that connection may I say I regret that under item 571 not one word was said by the Minister of National Defence with respect to

parliamentary review, other than by officers of the treasury board, of the defence research estimates in that section amounting to $14,495,861.
12.	That no members of Canada's armed forces, by virtue of such membership, shall be debarred from full exercise of the normal rights and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
13.	That the Canadian government establish crown companies for the sole manufacture and use of armaments, and that our ultimate aim be that such manufacture and use be under control by the united nations organization.
The members of our group feel that to implement the policy I have broadly outlined will be an effective way to realize Canada's duty to maintain the obligations toward world security under the united nations organization, provided further that our spokesmen at the conference press for early implementation of section 43 of the charter. Not one word has thus far come from the conference to the effect that Canada is vitally and honestly interested in securing implementation of section 43. Without this implementation the united nations will succeed no better than did the league of nations. The world wants no more national armaments, and the discovery of the atomic bomb has made national armaments a fallacy. Fighting forces are for attack only. Modern warfare makes the civilian population bear the whole brunt of defence, whether it be fire fighting, first aid or antiaircraft defences. The minister apparently is presenting no plan to prepare Canada for defence; therefore, if it be for attack, let it be according to plan of the united nations.
It was Pascal who said:
Strength without justice is tyrannical
And justice without strength is a mockery.

The hon. gentleman has made a very interesting speech. I agree with part of what he has said, and thank him for his support in reducing the number of brass hats. There are other suggestions with which I do not agree. The Department of National Defence is made up of men who are of the same type as those who were in charge during the first world war. I should qualify what I said about brass hats. Brass hats are men whom we see only in time of war. Beside that they are ignored and we do not know where they are. They are like rats which hide behind the walls and in time of war come out and eat the good Canadian cheese.
On occasion, sir, I have spoken outside the house, and I deeply regret the feeling that the eight provinces have against Quebec. I will explain to you, sir, why such feeling exists. It

Supply-National Defence
is precisely because of conscription. I congratulate the minister and his assistant on what has been done with regard to amnesty for soldiers and the draftees, but, as always, that measure is not entirely satisfactory to the men. In the first place it is unsatisfactory because it comes too late, and second because national registration was abolished at the same time that the amnesty was proclaimed. When I congratulated the hon. member for Lotbiniere on what he did with regard to the soldiers and draftees I told him that the amnesty proposal was apparently a good thing, but it was drafted in such ambiguous terms that no one could know what it meant; and it comes late. Now there is at least partial amnesty, or words mean nothing. Men who want to be discharged will get out of the camps at an early opportunity, but, sir, it was a long fight against conscription-but it was not described as military conscription. It was a long fight that was carried on; it was carried on mostly against prejudice which had been created by government; agencies, by the radio, by the vicious information board, and by all other means- propaganda to teach Canadians that their duty was to join the colours, and that if they did not do so they wTere not acting as good Canadian citizens.
The matter was taken up from a racial angle. The English-speaking members of the Quebec legislature were so silly as to say, I think with only one exception, "As we are of British allegiance w'e must be in favour of conscription," meaning military conscription. So it was put on a racial basis; the matter was discussed on those lines from beginning to end, on the stump, over the air, in the press, and all those who did not agree with that policy, which was exactly the same as the policy propounded by the brass hats in the first war, were not good citizens, not good Canadians. That was the policy; it was brought into the mind of everyone, one after the other. Everyone had to believe that the duty of all Canadians, and the only duty, was to join the colours; if he did not do so he was not doing well, he was not doing what he should. Here in this house, from the seat I occupied at the other end of the alley, I asked the Minister of Labour what was the duty of each Canadian citizen during the war. His answer was quick; he said his duty was to join the colours, to enlist in the army, and suggested that those who were not enlisting were not doing their duty. That was most absurd. There was a law; we had the Natural Resources Mobilization Act, to the effect that the boys should report to the registrar for medical examination, and that they should report to the camp when they were called by the registrar. They 63260-3171
did so; nevertheless they were covered with shame just because they were not enlisting. Those who were sick or unfit went in to enlist. Some of them were discharged at once, but they were considered1 as heroes just because they had signed a paper for overseas service.
The propaganda went on and on. There were full pages in the newspapers asking the boys to enlist, to do their duty. From the start a distinction was made between those who enlisted and those who did not, though they were complying with the law. That distinction was maintained. A button was given to those who had enlisted. Those who did not enlist could not get a job unless they had been discharged by the army for medical reasons. They were put aside; they were in a category by themselves; they were like the untouchables of India. Because some farmers believed in the promise made in this house by the Prime Minister himself that farmers would be exempted, a promise that was denied the following day by the Minister of Labour; because they took it for granted that the word of the Prime Minister was the solemn word of the government and of those in charge of the business of this country, those men were run after by army police and were given treatment that is a shame in a civilized country.
To come to my proposition, to the principle I was explaining, it is that there has been a vast amount of propaganda in this country to create the opinion, the same opinion that was created during the first war, that all men of military age who were physically fit should enlist in the army. After that was done; after all those who did not believe that the farmers, the railway men, the fishermen, the miners, those making munitions and arms, those making clothing and shoes for the soldiers, those working on ships at sea and building ships in the dockyards, should enlist were publicized as slackers; after some parents had lost children and friends in the war and there was a veil of mourning over the country, then it was said that conscription, the only thing that was needed for the prosecution of the war, was not imposed because of the province of Quebec. That is the type of propaganda that has been so strong in the other provinces against the province of Quebec, because in Quebec during the war the people kept their senses and thought exactly as I am sure all members of this committee now think. But during the war there was great excitement. Everybody was beating the drum; everybody was waving the flag. Then the opinion was different from what it is now, when the war is over. How many times have I and the other members who were fighting for the farmer been insulted and humiliated in this house, just because we had the firm conviction
Supply-National Defence

that the army alone, brave as it could be, could not win the war by itself. It deserved the help of all those men who were not slackers, all those men who were doing their duty. There is now a reaction, perhaps, in the minds of some people; but many still believe the province of Quebec is not the loyal province she actually is, that the province of Quebec has not done her duty, not because her sons did not enlist just the same as they abided by the law, but precisely because of that propaganda which has worked against the province of Quebec and which has been instigated by men who lived upon the money voted to support those who were m the fighting lines. It is most disgraceful; and it is precisely because that propaganda has been going on during five years of war that it will take a long time to redress the wrong that has been done to my native province in the minds of the Canadian people and in the minds of other nations as well. I ask the hon. gentlemen who are members of this house to think of us, to think how much the province of Quebec has suffered, precisely on account of the propaganda which has been instigated by a few men who are known as jingoes and junkers in this country.
We have been told many times that the province of Quebec was ruling the country, that everything was done to please that province. It was not true; the province of Quebec was slaughtered under the roses. The province of Quebec never had the influence to rule the government, because we had conscription when we were told there was no conscription. My hon. friend was not a minister of national defence during the war, but all ministers of national defence during war time, after the death of Hon. Norman Rogers, who had been a private during the first great war and who was a great man, were just the puppets of the brass hats, the junkers and jingoes who infest national defence headquarters at Ottawa. That is all they were. Ralston and McNaughton were just puppets of the men in N.D.H.Q.; no one can deny that. Those men at headquarters were ruling; they were the brass hats; they were the war lords; they were the war criminals. When I think of war criminals there is one I have to denounce to-day, and denounce bitterly. It is that man Chisholm, who made soldiers suffer so much during the war. And now Chisholm, shame to us, shame to the world, has been appointed to the united nations in charge of health. I wonder if he is playing a game of bingo at the casino Monte Carlo with the Minister of National Health and

Welfare at the present time. I do not know; it may be so. They are like Siamese twins; we cannot separate them.
But, Mr. Chairman, I receive abuse; I receive humiliation. I received it during the war, when I was alone, fighting for the railway men. There were members in the House of Commons who belonged to the unions; there were members in the House of Commons who were real labour men. But none of them raised his voice. I was surprised when the presidents of the two great railways said exactly what I have said on behalf of the railway men who were doing their duty in the war.
I could say much more, but I shall conclude by reading a letter I received to-day from a military organization. I shall not read all the letters I received. But when I fight for the men who are sometimes called the underdogs I do so in fulfilment of my duty. I fear no one in the fulfilment of that task. I consider that we in the House of Commons have a task to perform. I realize that there are progressive thoughts in the minds of my'hon. colleagues, even if they do not speak aloud, even if for one reason or another they do not dare to express themselves. But I know they are progressive, because otherwise they would not be so kind to me as they are now, and as they so often are.
This letter to which I have referred comes from the Canadian Combat Veterans' Association in British Columbia. It is dated at Vancouver, British Columbia, August 16, 1946, and says:
Jean Francois Pouliot, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Pouliot:-
I have just read your remarks recorded in the Hansard debates of August 1, 1946. I have particular reference to your pertinent observations concerning the defects in the administration of the Canadian (Military) Pension Act, pages 4154/4158 of the debates. You will, I know, well understand why this association assumed the responsibility of bringing to the attention of parliamentarians, of all political affiliations, the defaulting character of the administration in question. These conditions, as you well realize, have not grown up overnight but are implicit in the administration and call for the most drastic remedies.
On behalf of the membership of my association, who are men with actual service in a war theatre, without exception, I would like to express our very deep thanks for your courage in illustrating to parliament-by concrete cases- that, for some reason, justice does not freely operate for those who have sustained injury and disablement and handicap of ruined health as members of the armed forces of the nation. In so far as the criticism of the Minister of Veterans Affairs is concerned, interrupting your remarks, you may discount what he says, as while he is a man of very wide attainments of a scholastic nature, he is not representative of the

Supply-National Defence
front-line veterans of Canada, as his war-time history shows he was "temperamentally unfitted for front-line service" . . . With this knowledge, you will now perhaps understand why unnecessary evils have grown up in the administration in question as the outgrowth of political expediency rather than justice being honoured. I mention this fact in passing, but it is necessary you should possess- this information if you are to succeed in your endeavours in fighting for the under-privileged classes.
English-speaking Canadians who have seen service in either world wars I or II, hitherto have gathered the impression that little assistance would be forthcoming from French Canada in the herculean task of streamlining the administration of the legislation in question. Your stand, however, in the dominion parliament-the first of its kind-on these vital issues is a definite assurance to men like myself, representing influential groups of ex-servicemen, that the public opinion of French Canada is slowly but surely being oriented to the literally giganti* task of streamlining the process of justice, so that, in the very near future we may indeed build for our children and the generations who will follow us a democracy " of which no citizen need blush."_ Your address in parliament, if publicized, will be, I believe, a substantial factor in merging all men and women of goodwill to our common objectives of a Canada united in spirit and in truth, where injustice has no place. To-day, injustice is enthroned, and hence our national disunity.
From what has transpired in parliament, it is obvious there is a rising tide in the country led by able and fearless men who are determined that the peace is going to be won, where it can only be won, in the spiritual sphere, and that injustice, as such, has no place in the peace. As you so clearly point out, the call now is for men to stand on their feet for what is right and the Great Guidance will direct our path to the goal of a true Christian democracy.
Who signs that?

Walter H. Kirehner, secretary of the association. I could say much more than that; but, before closing, I wish to express my thanks to the minister for the interest he has taken in some cases which I have submitted to him; and my thanks also go to his able parliamentary assistant, who has shown patience in the correspondence I have had with him. But that correspondence would not have been necessary if we had not had in charge of some branches of the department men who were incompetent and unworthy of that office.
It is time to clear up the situation and to follow the suggestions already made by four members of parliament, three in connection with air services and one in connection with the army. It is time to make a check on the progress that is made, not in vague terms, but a check made to abolish some of the establishments. I know of some where the girls have been knitting since the close of the war, but they are receiving salaries just the same. The country has no need to pay them. I do not see why we should have any sympathy
for people whose task is over. They did very well during the war, but there is no more work for them. There are many men in the country who were faithful servants and helped do a job, but their job is over. Men should be set back, and women should be set back until there is another job.
I hope that war will never call for' more personnel in N.D.H.Q. than in any of the other war departments. I read that letter precisely to prove that point, and if I cannot secure the assistance of parliament I will get it from outside-and it will be very easy. I will get it, not from the officers of the last war-very few of them-but perhaps from some noncommissioned officers, and certainly from the soldiers in the ranks, those who have been outside and who want parliament to accomplish something.
Until now, what are memoers of parliament to say to their constituents, except that they [DOT] have passed a series of books of legislation, a Justinian review of past action by the parliament of Canada in the year 1946? We have passed legislation by the bushel. But the people are not interested in legislation, legislation that is passing in such quantity that no one can read it.
Tire people want reform, and I have tried for a long time to get it. In the interests of reform I have appealed to those who are Liberals and who call themselves Liberals. I thought their number was large enough to accomplish reform. But it is in the hands of the jingoes and the Junkers of N.D.H.Q., who were so well represented in parliament during the war by the megaphone of Arthur Meighen, when he was leader of the Conservative party.
I appealed first to the Liberals, and then I appealed to the Liberal-minded members of other groups in the house. Then I tried to do something for Canada, seeing that Canada was ignored, and that we should have a Canadian spirit-but without success. Party ties were too strong.
I now make an appeal for reform. Whether a man belongs to the Social Credit group, the C.C.F. group, or the Progressive Conservative party, and especially if he belongs to the Liberal party, he must have in his heart a strong desire for reform. I appeal to all those who are the grandsons or the great grandsons of reformers, and I ask them to listen to the voice of Canadians from coast to coast asking for reform in government, asking not for more government but for less government, and for more efficient and more competent government. This was my request, and it is not my yearly performance. It is a performance that I intend to give every time I have an opportunity to act here in accordance with

would hesitate very much to delay the progress of a very hard-working parliament; but in all my years in this house, and they are rather long now, I never listened to such twaddle in my life-twaddle-that is what it is. They have patriotic
hearts; they have fought for Canada, and I despise and condemn as strongly as I can the demagogic attack make by the hon. member for Temiscouata upon great Canadians. speechtext: I had not proposed to do so any more than I did on the naval estimates. Since the opportunity to debate defence matters has been rather limited during this session I should like to make a few remarks on the army's role in defence generally and to keep them as applicable to these estimates as possible.
I imagine that a large proportion of the moneys that are to be voted in these estimates has to do with the demobilization of the personnel and 'the cleaning up of various bills outstanding. I think I would be voicing the opinion of members on all sides of the house when I say that we were pleased that the demobilization has been carried out as expeditiously as possible and we rejoice with those people in the country who are welcoming back their loved ones who have been overseas. Generally speaking, I do not think there is any doubt that demobilization has been carried out as expeditiously as it was reasonable to expect. We realize the difficulties there have been regarding shipping, and if there have been some disappointments with personnel not being home as soon as was expected, in the great majority of cases perhaps these were unreasonable expectations.
There are, however, or two points in connection with the demobilization programme which have not met with the entire approval of the country. It will be remembered that last session members from this side of the

house urged a more general application of the principle that those who had seen the longest and hardest service be returned to Canada first. We realize that it was not possible to carry out entirely the principle of "first in, first out". But we feel that more consideration might have been given to the proposal which was made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard that those men who were entitled to wear campaign medals should be given a greater degree of priority in being brought back.
There is a group of men to whom I feel special reference should be made, and those are the individuals who have been referred to as key personnel. I refer to the clerks, the provost corps, the cooks, and a certain number of officers, regimental and staff. I should also like to express regret that it was found necessary to demobilize entirely, I believe-I can go only by press reports-the C.W.A.C. Those girls in the service did remarkable work. The majority of them are also anxious to return to their homes. But some were willing to stay on in the service. I believe it would- have been well worth while maintaining a small nucleus of girls in the service upon which we could build, and so develop the experience in the years to come that, in the event of the unhappy circumstances arising again of Canada being plunged into war and our having to utilize the woman power of the country, we should not have to go through the difficulties which we met with, owing to lack of experience in the middle of this last war when the C.W.A.C. was first organizing. There are many branches of the army work which women can undertake, and the chances are that by study and experience in times of peace we could, find that, if another war broke out, the women of the country would be better prepared to take their place in the ranks with the men than they were during this war.
One other aspect of demobilization to which I should like to make reference is the position of the permanent force personnel who, by means of their satisfactory service during the war, gained promotion and now find, in some cases, that they have to resign their commissions and join the ranks, if they still wish to stay on, at a very much lower grade of rank than they had earned during the war. I
realize that in many cases it would be necessary for officers and non-commissioned officers to step down a rank or two, but it is difficult for the man who has earned a commission on the field of battle and has perhaps risen to the rank of captain to find, when he wants to continue his service in order that he may reap the benefit of the pension to which he regards himself as entitled, that he will have to step down in some cases to almost the lowest ranks in the army.
One other aspect which has some connection with demobilization, and to which I referred earlier in the session, is the withdrawal of the Canadian occupational force from Germany.
I feel that some criticism on that action should be advanced, or at least that we should demand a full explanation-an explanation which the Prime Minister promised when I raised the question some months ago-as to why that force was withdrawn at that time. There was a feeling, expressed in a Gallup poll which was held some months ago, that Canada was in some measure abandoning her responsibilities in the great and vital task of the recivilization of Germany, in years when the German people would have to decide whether they would adopt a form of democracy or some form of totalitarian government. I realize that men who had had long service in the field would be anxious to return home and might be loath to continue their service in the occupational forces. A certain number of volunteers was obtained for the purpose of providing the numbers to which Canada had agreed. Other men were detailed for that duty from the establishments in Europe or in England. But apparently there were not sufficient personnel available to make up the numbers which were required, without imposing hardships on men who had seen a good deal of fighting. There is the feeling amongst some of our allies, which to a certain extent was expressed in the British House of Commons, that perhaps this country, which had never let down any of its allies during the war, was rather letting them down during this critical stage, the early days of peace. When it was suggested that it was hard that our allies should have to bear the burden alone, the reason advanced for our withdrawal was, I understand, that it was for administrative reasons. If Canada hopes to hold a position and to carry out any commitments whifih the united nations may call upon her to do in the future, we must learn how to overcome "administrative difficulties".
Leaving that: on a question of general policy, it has not been easy for the members of this house to follow the general pattern of our defence policy, because many of the announcements regarding policy and the
Supply-National Defence

developments which are to follow have been made outside this house, and it is only by press reports that one has been able to glean information in the endeavour to patch the pieces together so that one might get the over-all picture. But I gather that it is the policy of the government, a policy with which I feel all parties will agree, that Canada must take every practical step which is po^ible to defend her own territory and to be prepared to meet any obligations which may be assigned to her by the united nations organization when their defence committee starts to function properly. I believe the country as a whole is anxious to support such a policy. The country realizes that we are close to a great war, the issue of which at times was very much in the balance. The country also realizes that modern armaments cost a great deal of money: huge expenses are required for modern equipment in the air force, in the navy and in the army. I do not believe that our people would object to voting the sums which are necessary, but they want to be absolutely certain that the money is being spent as judiciously as possible and in a way which may be expected to achieve the results for which it is voted.
In order to ensure the efficiency of our fighting forces, during the last session hon. members on this side of the house made certain suggestions. It will be remembered that the hon. member for Vancouver South suggested that there be a standing committee , on questions of defence, made up from all parties in this house. When that suggestion was repeated at the beginning of this session the Prime Minister made remarks to the effect that he thought that might be a very good idea. However, nothing has happened. We have urged that there should be a closer coordination of the three services. I cannot help feeling that there is no evidence that there is a closer coordination at the present time. There is on the order paper a resolution to continue the two ministers of defence. Well, an argument may be put forward for retaining a minister for air for a limited period while demobilization is going on and while the air force is readjusting itself to peacetime conditions. But if we are to have any common doctrine between the three services,
I think the first step should be to get those services under one minister.
As other indications of lack of determination to have the three services properly coordinated, I suggest the location of some of the headquarters of the new commands is indicative that the importance of a close liaison between the different services is not fully realized. I can refer only to conditions on the

Pacific coast. During the war, the army, the navy and the air force all had their headquarters at Jericho beach in Vancouver. These headquarters have dispersed. The air force remains at Jericho; the navy has gone over to Esquimalt, and the army has gone to Edmonton. A similar condition exists on the Atlantic coast. There may be administrative reasons for this, but it seems to me that it gives one the impression that perhaps the great importance of a close liaison between all the services is not fully appreciated.
Another point which was emphasized during the last session was the recommendation I made myself that, in order to ensure as far as possible that we drew up the right pattern for our defence forces, the heads of the services, the heads of industry and of the professions and sciences, should be assembled to form what I referred to as a Canadian Haldane committee in order to decide the general pattern for the three defence services. None of these recommendations was adopted. One is almost forced to the conclusion that perhaps the government has failed to realiize the effect of the development of new weapons and of changing conditions, and the effect that should have upon the position of our forces, with the result that to-day the government is committing the nation to a long-range programme of heavy expenditure without having fully realized the new position in which, I suggest, Canada now finds herself.
That new condition, I suggest, is this. Prior to the outbreak of this war. Canada's defence policy -had for many years been based on the assumption that, if -war broke out, she would be required to send a force overseas to fight what I may describe as an empire war, certainly a war fought in conjunction with other empire forces, somewhere other than on the North American continent. For years it has been our proud boast that we have not had to defend our southern frontier, that our relationships with the United States have been so satisfactory that it has -been quite unnecessary for us to make any real preparations against the possibility of attack by our neighbour to the south.
Therefore it has been possible for the general staffs so to arrange their organization, so to arrange their plans, that the main purpose of the Canadian defence forces would be to take part in a war, not in Canada but in some other part of the world. The years 1914 and 1939 bear out the efficiency with which, those plans were made, and their effectiveness. Those plans were based mainly on the assumption that there would be a period of rather leisurely mobilization and a period of further training which would be available to the troops that

Supply-National Defence
Canada was going to send overseas. And as in 1914 there were many weeks before the Canadian troops were actually engaged, so in this war, in 1939 and 1940, there were fortunately many months before our forces were required to be battle-worthy.
I wonder if these conditions exist to-day. If one stops to ponder for only a moment, he is forced to the conclusion that there are only three powers which could possibly launch this world into world war III-the British commonwealth of nations, the United States and the Soviet Republic of Russia. You may take any combination of those three powers you like, and it is inevitable that Canada then becomes a major theatre of war and that Canada's shores are on the highway between any of the combinations of these opponents. There would foe no time for leisurely mobilization; there would be no question of sending troops away from our shores. If the tragedy of world war III comes, then world war III is going to be fought in Canada. Therefore our Canadian organization for defence must foe based on the premise that we have to fight here, and we have in peace time to make our plans, not for the same leisurely mobilization, not for that period of training after the outbreak of hostilities, but for an organization which will be able to stop the bomber from coming to Canadian targets without warning.
That, I submit, requires most careful thought before we commit the country to any type of defence forces which does not have that primary factor as the first consideration for the organization which is prepared in peace time. As I say, we have never had an over-all picture; but I am forced to the conclusion, from the information I gather from the press, that the government's policy is not visualizing any great departure from that policy which has stood us in such good stead under entirely different circumstances in the past. We are still basing our peacetime army organization on an increased nonpermanent militia and an increased permanent [DOT] force. I see in these plans, in what I know of the type of unit which has been authorized either for the permanent force or for the nonpermanent militia or reserve army, as it is now being called, little which would indicate that it will be ready to meet a sudden attack on Canadian shores, launched with the new weapons of the scientific era.
I feel, so far as details are concerned, that they will make the non-permanent militia a little bit brighter and a little bit bigger, but I am afraid that the non-permanent militia officer has still to makfe great sacrifices both in time and in money. He will find that he will have to devote a great deal of his time 63260-318
to bringing the units up to strength. His efforts will be largely devoted to recruiting and holding the men by social activities rather than to training the men to take the field at a quick and early notice. I feel that while the proposals, as far as I can gather them from the press reports, indicate that the permanent force is to be divided into what I should call three sections; one, to look after the administration ; two, to be central schools and, three, to be a brigade group or a small field force, that field force at the present moment is terribly under strength; it is short of equipment; its armour is obsolescent and the units will be starved of trained personnel in exactly the same way as they were starved during the years between the two wars.
The field force is referred to as a brigade group. A brigade group is not a modern formation, although the grouping of certain specialized units might be referred to as a brigade group. The whole virtue of brigading together certain units was that the personnel of these units would be familiar one with the other and would be exercised in working together.
A few weeks ago I asked the Minister of National Defence whether these units were to be concentrated or distributed across the country. I suppose, for administrative reasons, he said that they were to be distributed across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I fear that we are going back to the same old story of little companies of permanent force troops at various provincial capitals prepared to put on a guard at the opening of the legislatures, prepared to provide some sort of little display at county fairs and so forth. If we are to have a field force which is to be of any value at all, that force must be concentrated and trained together so that one may know the other. Skeleton formations will not be the answer to these sudden attacks.
I have grave doubts as to the effectiveness of the grouping of these units. We have not been told exactly which units are to form the permanent force. Again one can only get the information from the press reports. I feel that this field force is woefully short of the technical units. During the last years of the war just ended, the principles which were enunciated by such great leaders as Alexander, Montgomery and Crerar were for the overwhelming concentration of supporting arms behind a small group of infantry or armour which conducted a penetration on narrow fronts. From what I can learn of the organization of this field force, it is lacking in the technical units and in the supporting arms which would be able to adhere to this policy.
To date, I think one must admit that the numbers joining the permanent force and the

Supply-National Defence

numbers of those who are in the interim force and have expressed a desire to join the permanent force are disappointing. I do not know why that is. On the whole, the new rates of pay are satisfactory. The standard of education which is required of perhaps both officers and men may hardly be practicable of achievement.
In regard to the various items in the estimates, there will be some room for criticism in regard to administration particularly. There is justifiable questioning as to whether this new command organization will make the necessary reductions in personnel in the districts and in national defence headquarters which one would believe that it was designed to do. We cannot have greater commands superimposed upon the districts unless we see a reduction in the number of personnel either in these districts and subordinate staffs or in the staffs at national headquarters.
In conclusion, I am forced to say that I believe the organization is faulty because the government has not taken a realistic view of the up-to-date requirements of the type of defence which Canada needs to-day, which is not the type of defence organization that was in vogue twenty-five years ago. I doubt whether the government has realized the danger of modern warfare. Therefore I feel that some of the expenditures in these estimates are definitely wasteful and unwarranted because they will fail to be effective.

I understand a commonwealth military conference was held in Britain last week, presided over by Field Marshal Montgomery. I wonder if the minister is prepared to say what were the problems discussed there, what policies, if any, were agreed upon, and whether Canada was represented at such conference.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that I would call it a commonwealth military conference. What did take place was that Field Marshal Montgomery was having a meeting with his chiefs of staff and senior officers, and invited our chief of the general staff to attend. No questions of policy were discussed; it was not a conference at which matters of policy were to be discussed. It was more an exposition of tactical problems and a general discussion of matters of that kind. It was not a discussion of matters of policy, but a general roundtable conference, discussion or exposition of modern tactical procedure. The chief of the general staff returned this morning. I understand that at the same time Sir Arthur Tedder held a discussion with his senior air officers. The chief of the air staff was invited to attend that conference, and did so.

I was hoping that on item I the minister would say something with regard to the Royal Military College at Kingston. Since he did not do so, perhaps he would answer one or two questions in that connection. First, why was the Royal Military College at Kingston closed for the training of gentleman cadets? When was it closed? On whose authority was it closed, and when does his department expect to reopen it? If the minister would answer those questions I shall have one or two more to ask later.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not recall just when it was closed, but it was during the war, I think in 1940 or 1941. The question as to when it will be reopened and under what circumstances, has, as my hon. friend knows, been brought up in the house on a number of occasions. In answering the various questions I indicated that it was the intention of the government to continue the Royal Military College, but that under what conditions had not been determined. In order to assist me and the officers of my department in arriving at a sound conclusion in that respect, a special committee was set up under the chairmanship of a distinguished soldier, Brigadier Sherwood Lett of Vancouver. That committee completed its hearings in July; there was prepared and submitted to me some two or three weeks later a report, which I now have and which is being studied. It is an excellent report, which I found extremely interesting and which is going to be of great assistance. I am not yet in a position to state on just what basis the Royal Military College will be reopened. I announced, of course, that it would not be reopened on the old basis this fall. We have ample supplies of officers, for the moment, for our post-war forces. I hope to be able to make an announcement perhaps before parliament reconvenes; but, if not, certainly at the latest before the end of the next session.

I wish to impress upon the minister as strongly as I can the fact that the public are expecting an announcement, and I think that announcement should have been made this session. It is now getting late in August. I do not agree, with what the minister has said. He did not answer my question, on whose recommendation the college was closed for the training of gentleman cadets, whether it was the recommendation of the chief of staff or of the committee. It was not closed in the last war, but it was closed during this war. I am informed, though I believe there is a difference of opinion in that regard, that the closing of the college was a mistake. Many young men across Canada are to-day

Supply-National Defence
being deprived of the opportunity of attending the Royal Military College because, as the minister and his officers well know, a young man cannot enter the college when he is nineteen, twenty or twenty-one. It is these boys of sixteen, seventeen and eighteen who are losing that opportunity. For that reason, if the committee will bear with me for a moment, I should like to place on record something of what the college has done. I do so because only a few days ago we in Kingston celebrated our 100th anniversary of the founding of the city, and for seventy years the Royal Military College has played an important part, not only in the life of that city, but in the life of the whole country.
The motto of the Royal Military College is "truth, duty, valour." This challenging motto is the anvil upon which the destinies of gentlemen cadets have been shaped since 1876 at the Royal Military College, Kingston. The carefully kept records of graduates' careers tell something of the success the Royal Military College in preparing Canadian youth for tasks of leadership, but the sum. total can never be stated. If the purpose of the founding of the college was to train young men in the profession of arms in order to provide leadership in times of national crises, then that purpose has been and is continuing to be served.
Following an enviable record in the first great war, the cadets and ex-cadets brought even more honours to their college with their service in the second conflict. A total of 1,419 cadets were engaged in service, including sixty-two who were doing special war work. One hundred and; thirteen gave their lives in action, 637 awards and honours to R.M.C. alumni have been announced to date. The Victoria Cross was won by Lieut.-Colonel Cecil Merritt, the George Cross by Air Commodore A. D. Ross, and a Companion of Honour by General H. D. G. Crerar. As a result of their service in the second conflict, knighthoods were awarded to four ex-cadets: Lieut-General Sir G. N. Cory, K.C.B.; Lieut-General Sir A. E. Grasett, K.B.E.; Brigadier C. F. Carson and Brigadier E. O. Wheeler, the last of whom is the present surveyor general of India. Commander of the Bath was awarded to fifteen graduates, Commander of the British Empire to fifty-five, and Distinguished Service Order to seventy-seven. Other awards included sixty-nine foreign orders. A total of 199 ex-cadets held the rank of colonel or above in the army or equivalent rank in other services. Altogether 280 graduates of the college have attained such rank since the college was founded. Twenty-nine attained the standing of general in the second 63260-3181
war, twenty-eight in previous wars. This number includes those serving in both the British and Canadian armies and in other services.
The first step in the history of the college was the passing of an act to establish a military college in one of the garrison towns of Upper Canada by the imperial parliament in May, 1874. The Royal Military College was founded in 1876 by Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, then, prime minister of Canada. The linking of Alexander Mackenzie's name with the R.M.C. recalls one of the delightful bits of personal history from the early years of Canada's development. Thirty years before his choice of the site for the college, Mr. Mackenzie was employed as a stone mason on the self-same site when Fort Frederick was being erected. As he worked he could see the great natural beauty of the site as well as its strategic position in the military scheme, so what more natural than to select it for a military training school when he became prime minister?
Cadets have come to Kingston from all parts of Canada and, upon graduating, all have entered for a time into a life of duty to the country and to the empire in the military, air and police forces. The story of their exploits in the interests of the great commonwealth is a wonderful one. Mention might be made of a few; of Girouard and Rhodes in South Africa; of Bridges, the first G.O.C. of the Australians in the first great war and founder of the R.M.C. of Australia; of Luard and Straubenzee in China and Malaya; of Kirkpatrick, Heneker, Cory, Nanton, Lotbiniere in India; of Perry, Sanders and Macdonnell in the R.C.M.P.; of Stairs who died in 1892 while with the H. M. Stanley expedition in Africa; of Massey-Baker in Papua; of Bishop, Twining and Burstall, Macdonnell and Panet; names to conjure with during the heroic struggle of 1914 to 1918.
During world war II, former cadets held strategic positions on all fronts. General Sir G. D. Rhodes, C.B., C.B.E., D.S.O., was in charge of military transportation in Iran from the Persian gulf to the Caspian sea. At the same time Brigadier Sir C. F. Carson, C.BE., M.C., also an R.M.C. graduate, was directing similar activities in Iran.
Two chiefs of general staff of the Canadian army, Lieutenant-General K. Stuart, C.B., D.S.O., M.C., and Lieutenant-General J. C. Murchie, C.B., C.B.E., are also graduates of the college, as are Major General J. V. Young, C.B., C.B.E., and Major General J. H. MacQueen, C.B.E., masters general of ordnance, and Major General N. E. Rodger, C.B.E.,

Supply-National Defence
quartermaster-general of the Canadian army. Major General Chris Yokes is also a graduate of the famed military college.
Though the teaching at the college has been primarily for the purpose of training officers for the army, the accomplishments of its graduates are by no means limited to the military field.
Amongst those, past and present, who have achieved distinction in civilian capacities are: Sir Percy Girouard, one-time governor of the East African Protectorate; Lieutenant-General Sir A. E. Grasett, lieutenant-governor of the Isle of Jersey; Colonel P. C. H. Primrose, one-time lieutenant-governor of Alberta; Colonel Colin Gibson, present air minister; Major-General A. B. Perry, C.M.G., former commissioner and S. T. Wood, C.M.G., present commissioner of the R.C.M.P.; F. H. Peters, former surveyor-general for Canada; Lieutenant-Colonel R. E. Kent, alderman and several times mayor of the city of Kingston; R. T. M. Scott, and W. Heighington, well-known writers of fiction, and numerous other lawyers, doctors, engineers, editors and industrial men.
For many years the command of the college was held by imperial officers, but that practice was discontinued in 1919. The present commandant is Brigadier J. D. B. Smith, C.B.E., D.S.O.
The grounds comprise a peninsula between Kingston harbour and Navy bay and consist of about forty acres. The buildings are grouped on three sides of the square. The oldest and most historic building is the "Stone Frigate", a dormitory, and one of the original buildings of the old naval yard; the newest is the mess hall and gymnasium. At the entrance to the grounds on highway No. 2 is the memorial arch, erected by the R.M.C. club in 1923. This is undoubtedly one of the finest memorials in America. The splendid sturdiness and strength of its aspect dominate the approach to the college. Its panels in bold relief, its groupings of military attributes, its helmeted head sculptured on the keystone, its inscriptions and tablets-all will repay close inspection. The arch is a fitting memorial to the memory of former cadets who died in the first world war.
The college has accommodation for 200 students, and it was planned to have the "Stone Frigate" supplanted by a modern dormitory adjoining the new mess hall. The excavations in solid rock had been made for the new dormitory, when all work at the college was suspended in favour of more urgent activities following the outbreak of war in 1939.

I thank hon. members for giving me their attention, and I have placed these facts on the record only because I believe some recognition is due the Royal Military College. Therefore I make no apology in offering my appeal to the minister. I suggest if the Royal Military College is not used, why is Royal Roads being used for boys in the navy.
Before taking my seat, I should like to refer to two other matters which affect my riding of Kingston. First, I would associate myself with other hon. members who have referred to the manner in which the minister's staff, or some in the department, are dealing with men who are returning from overseas and who wish to join the permanent force. There is something wrong about this. The men I have in mind enlisted in the permanent force before the war, and perhaps served for five or ten years before going overseas. I have in mind one man particularly who joined the army as a profession. He was in the R.C.H.A. when war broke out, and proceeded overseas, first as a lance-sergeant, and then, after getting overseas, receiving his command as a subaltern. Following that, he was promoted to the rank of captain. This man, in his early thirties, led a battery in France during the present war.
This man is now back here, and I am asking the minister what he is going to do for him. I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs will agree with me that in our committee on veterans affairs which passed on twelve pieces of legislation we had to ask civilian employers to take some of these men from the service. When they come back, and show a desire to continue in the permanent force, they are told that they must lose their commission. Surely there is something wrong with that. Surely a man in his early thirties should not be asked to revert to a lower rank, particularly when there is no guarantee of employment in civilian life. This setup is wrong. I know there are various depots across Canada manned by men who are new in the service.
Then, these men who are making then-applications are orphans. The R.C.H.A. is established at Petawawa, and a man going to the depot must be paraded before his officer commanding, only to find that he must leave the service. And what is happening at Petawawa is happening everywhere. No one is acting for these men, with the result that, as I have said, they are orphans. A man with fifteen years' service before the war comes back from overseas, and expresses a desire to give more service.
Then, when a man is put back in the ranks, what happens? This man has gone out to fight for Canada and the empire, but upon returning to his own country he finds that he must

Supply-National Defence
become a junior to some officer or non-commissioned officer or warrant officer, and must take instructions from him.
I appeal to the minister to issue instructions so that this may be changed. I am afraid there are too many young men on the general staff to-day who are not taking a kindly or fatherly interest in these returning men.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are trying to build up. an efficient army.

I say that the minister should find appointments for these men who came back from the last war. It should not be difficult to find a place for a man who has been a competent officer-and I am not referring to those who have been incompetent. Surely there should be some place for them in the interim army.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are accused of having too many officers.

A reply to a question I put on the order paper shows that ten per cent of the officers in the army at the present time did not serve outside Canada. There are ten per cent with the rank of subaltern and five per cent with the rank of captain who, I say, have places found for them. Someone looked after these men. Men who rendered service in the permanent force and during the war have been replaced by them.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the house rose at six o'clock I had been speaking of the Royal Military College at Kingston and of returning permanent force officers who had fought gallantly overseas and who are not now getting the breaks they should get. Some of them are in their early thirties, and if they could continue in the service for another four or five years they would be eligible for pension. Employers of labour are compelled, under legislation parliament has passed, to reinstate their civilian employees who have returned from overseas service, and I submit to the minister that his department should set the example in looking after these returning permanent force officers. The same question was raised when the Royal Canadian Mounted Police estimates were before the committee. Some of these permanent force officers returning from overseas have lost promotions which they should not have lost, and that fact
should be recognized. Some of them have had fifteen years' experience in the army, and surely they should receive more consideration than a boy who has been in the service for only four or five years. Instructions should be issued to the general staff that these men deserve and should receive more consideration than they are getting.
I also want to say a word or two about bands for the permanent force. What is the policy of the department in that matter? Are the bands being demobilized, or is it intended to continue them? Personally I think they should be continued. I think we should have a band to every one thousand or fifteen hundred men in the interim army. Back in the dark days in the 1940's the bands were being dismissed. It was a shame and disgrace to whoever was administering the army at that time to let the bands go out of existence, and a great deal of credit is due to the units themselves in maintaining bands out of the canteen funds. But I do not think we should have to depend on the militia units across Canada to maintain the bands, and I should like to know what the policy of the department is in regard to them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think I have already said all I can say at the moment as to future policy with respect to the Royal Military College. I agree wholeheartedly with what my hon. friend has said as to the outstanding record which has been, won for the college by its graduates. They have served w'ith distinction in the two great wars in the last thirty years, and what my hon. friend said was certainly no overstatement of the magnificent record which the graduates of the college have won for themselves.
As to ithe promotion of permanent force non-commissioned officers and other ranks during the war, there has been some criticism on the other side of the matter, namely, that promotions have been too rapid and too great and that a good many permanent force noncommissioned officers have been retired on substantial pensions which in some respects are out of proportion to the rank which they held at the beginning of the war. I know that what my hon. friend is referring to are the permanent non-commissioned officers now in their early thirties who in some cases have been found unsuitable by the selection committee as commissioned officers in the postwar army. Any minister of national defence, indeed any minister, is obliged to rely on the advice of his officers, and a selection committee was set up for the selection of personnel to form part of the post-war force. I would not for one moment constitute myself
Supply-National Defence

a one-man selection committee for the postwar army. That would be most improper. But I have looked into the question of the selection of officer personnel for post-war army, and in a number of cases where permanent force non-commissioned officers have not been found suitable for retention in their present rank I find that in every case they have been given the opportunity of reverting to the rank they held before the war. It is understandable that some of them would not be suitable for the post-war army. In war time there is a largely expanded personnel and one can use a great many officers in operational duty who, by reason of educational standards or otherwise, are not suitable for the comparatively small number of highly specialized officers required in peace time. That is the case with a good many of the permanent force non-commissioned officers to whom my hon. friend has referred. It has been found that, by reason of educational standards or in a great many cases lack of operational experience, they are not suitable for retention in the post-war army. We must proceed on the assumption that, with a small army for the post war, we must make that army as efficient as possible, and we cannot afford to be influenced by consideration of sentiment. We must endeavour to get the ablest and most suitable material that we can possibly get for the officer corps. Unfortunately, because we had such a small army prior to the outbreak of the last war, we were obliged to use a great many permanent force non-commissioned officers as instructional officers in Canada. AVe have a great many officers who, through no fault of their own, were not able to see overseas service. We had to keep them in Canada for instructional purposes. I can only answer my hon. friend's plea that consideration should 'be given to this class of soldier by saying that it is being given and that the selection committee for officers in the post-war army is doing its best to see that the officers selected are the very best possible, taking into account educational qualifications, operational experience and the like.
On the subject of bands I agree with my hon. friend that it is extremely important that there should be adequate bands. Through no one's fault in particular it was felt early in the war that bands were not necessary, but that lack was early recognized and I can assure my hon. friend that we will see that proper provision is made in the post-war army for a suitable number of bands.

Thus far no member of the Social Credit group has had anything to say on this occasion in regard to defence,

not because we are not intensely interested in the subject. I believe that many Canadians are in grave danger of becoming unrealistic toward the matter of defence. I was alarmed when I heard the speech of the hon. member for Regina city, because it indicated that there is already developing in a considerable number of people a tendency to become victims of phantasy regarding matters of defence. Here are we, Canadians, eleven and a half or twelve millions of us; we have the finest land on earth, stretching thousands and thousands of miles. That land has to be defended. Someone must defend it. There are only three ways in which it can be defended.
One is by our cooperating with the members of the British commonwealth, the greatest team for defence of freedom the world has ever known; another is by cooperation with the United States and the other American countries in a scheme for western hemispheric defence; or, standing alone and trying to defend ourselves. There are a good many who will be somewhat offended because I have left out of consideration the united nations organization. I do not hesitate a minute to say before this house, and before the country in so far as anyone is interested in what I say, that the united nations organization is going to be just as useful in defending the peace of the world as the league of nations was, and no more. So that, if we rely on that organization, we shall by just so much betray the trust which is placed upon us in this fateful time. That is the point of view which Social Crediters take.
I was very much pleased with the speech delivered by the hon. member for Nanaimo. It indicated a disposition to face facts as they are; it indicated that the speaker knew what he was talking about, that he was living in a world of realities and intending to face that world realistically. I think we Social Crediters must associate ourselves with the words of the hon. member.
As I recall it, the minister stated that our navy is to be prepared to cooperate effectively either with the United States or with Great Britain. I assume that the minister has a similar aim as regards the Canadian army and the Canadian air force. I gather that the minister plans to make each of our three fighting services into a high-grade, efficient fighting unit, a unit adapted to defend our country with the greatest measure of striking power economically possible for Canada as a nation. AVith such a policy the Social Credit party is fully in agreement; and I wish to assure the minister that, in going forward with the responsibilities of his exceedingly difficult task, so long as he continues to face in the direction

Supply-National Defence
he now is facing and so long as he continues to go forward with " full speed ahead", he will have our complete support.

I hope I may be pardoned if I say a few words regarding a matter which was discussed this morning, namely, in connection with the services at Dieppe to-day. I had an opportunity about- eighteen months ago of being in the town of Dieppe. I saw the graves that were spoken of this morning, of the men who died there; I saw the beach on which they died; and I saw the hills and fortifications surrounding that beach. I am not going to elaborate on this, but the thought occurred to me then and it has occurred to me many times since, that the sacrifice which was made there was hardly worth while for the information that was obtained. I felt then and I feel now, that the price which was paid for that information was too high, and I believe it could have been obtained by other means. As a surprise attack, I think the operation would have been impossible: with the surprise element gone- and we all know the Germans knew our men were in the English channel and about to attack-it did appear to me, and I am sure it must have done to a great many, that the task they were asked to accomplish was almost as hopeless and possibly as brilliant as the charge of the Light Brigade.
I agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge in the statement he made regarding the hon. member for Nanaimo. I listened to his statement this afternoon: it was one of the best summing-up of any situation, military or other, which I have heard in this house. We of the House of Commons are fortunate to have a member with the practical experience in military matters of the hon. member for Nanaimo. Few men in Canada have his experience or -his knowledge of such problems, and this house and the country should be very grateful for the information which he has given us this afternoon. He outlined the situation; and I congratulate the hon. member for Lethbridge upon his very short speech in which he also outlined the situation as we see it in Canada. He mentioned what he regards as the two alternatives. Well, we live in a time of hope, though possibly in years to come it may seem like wishful thinking. But I am not one of those who despair of the united nations; I hope and1 expect that they will accomplish something as far as world peace is concerned. If they do not, it will be a very sad thing indeed for this world. We can only wait and see; we should know in a few months what the situation will be as regards the united
nations' programme, and what are to be the military commitments as far as Canada is concerned to the organization. If we have full assurance from the united nations and are satisfied that their ideas are practical, perhaps we can then base our defence programme upon w'hat we learn at that time. But there are two other alternatives, as -has been mentioned here. The first is, coordination and work with the British commonwealth of nations. We have cooperated with the British commonwealth in two great wars, and I wish to say here that I feel, and I know practically every hon. member and everybody in Canada feels, that we were justified in entering both of those wars, that we -had to enter them not only for the defence of our country but in defence of the ideals for which we stand. We cooperated, as I say, with the British commonwealth of nations. In the future, whether we have a united nations' programme or whatever we have, the British commonwealth of nations must stick together, and our entry or whatever our contribution is to the united nations should be more or less upon a commonwealth programme.
I might also say that if it had not been for the unity of the British empire and the British commonwealth of nations in the early part of the recent war it is doubtful whether we would have the freedom we enjoy to-day; and had not England, Canada, Australia and New Zealand fought for that freedom in 1941 it is unlikely that the United States or even Russia would be in the position in which they are at this time. The empire saved the world.
The third alternative is cooperation with the United States. Well, we can cooperate with the United States as a commonwealth of nations; and if the- British commonwealth of nations and the United States stand together, the freedom of the world will be assured whether we have a united nations' programme which is satisfactory or whether we do not.
My main object in rising was to obtain from the minister, if I could, information regarding a matter which I know has occupied the minds of a good many people in recent months. It was reported here some months ago that either the parliament of Great Britain or the war department there, I do not know which, had put out feelers to see whether Great Britain could train troops in Canada. We remember that a few years before the war it was definitely stated that Great Britain had asked to be allowed to train airmen in this country. I know it was denied in this house that Great Britain had made that request. I am satisfied that
Supply-National Defence

she did not make the request, because countries do not make requests, even sister countries in the British commonwealth of nations. But I am also satisfied that some intimation was given that Britain would like to have trained airmen in this country before the last war. Limited as she was in her own borders, with her small area, it was only logical and reasonable that she would like to train her airmen in some country where there were greater opportunities for the purpose. I ask definitely now: Has Great Britain in any way intimated that she would like to train troops in Canada? I can see the benefit it would be to us.
The hon. member for Nanaimo this afternoon demonstrated logically to the committee, as I am sure he has demonstrated to the rest of the country, that the world situation to-day being what it is, if another great war broke out our soldiers would be fighting, not on the continent of Europe or in some other part of the world. We can reasonably expect that in such an event they would be fighting here on their own soil and in defence of their own country. What greater asset would there be in the defence of this country if a sister nation like Great Britain or Australia, or any other sister nation within the commonwealth, had men trained in this country, men who had been acclimatized here, men who knew the terrain, the climate and the people?
If Great Britain has not asked to be allowed to train troops here, it would not be out of place for Canada to suggest that she might do so. We have the report, and it is in the press, that having failed to obtain this opportunity in Canada, Great Britain is sending troops to Australia for training, where there are large areas and great opportunities for combined and operational training.
We have been jealous of our sovereignty in Canada. We have heard a good deal about that. I remember in 1938, one of the reasons advanced why Canada could not allow Great Britain to train her airmen here was that it affected the sovereignty of the dominion. Well, Australia is not afraid of her sovereignty. We did not lose our sovereignty because airmen from all parts of the commonwealth trained here during the war, and we shall not lose our sovereignty if Great Britain or any other sister nation of the commonwealth trains men here during peace time. I am not going to labour this point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will answer it as soon as you are through.

I expect the minister to answer it. The hon. member for Nanaimo spoke about wars to-day not having the acquisition of territory in view. That is very true. 
In the old wars one nation, for territorial or other reasons, fought another, taking away part of its territory. The last war, however, was fought between fascism and nazism on the one hand and democracy on the other. If there are wars in the future they will be more for the purpose of advancing some ideology than for the purpose of acquiring territory; and if we wish to preserve, as I know we all do, our present way of living, then the nations that love freedom and democracy must combine to work hand in hand in every way possible to preserve their freedom and their ideals.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member for Royal has brought up the question of the training of United Kingdom troops in Canada, because I saw the press reports to which he has referred. May I make the statement that there has never been any request, formal or informal, that United Kingdom troops should be allowed to train in Canada. A wreek or so after these reports appeared in the paper, Major-General Keightley, who is director of training for the British army, was in Canada; we had an opportunity of discussing the matter with him, both the members of my staff and myself personally, and he definitely ruled out any question of British troops training in Canada. In saying that, I do not preclude for one moment the exchange of personnel, which I hope will take place between our forces and those of the United Kingdom; but I am glad of this opportunity to dispel once and for all these rumours that the Canadian government has been requested to allow United Kingdom troops to train in Canada and has not allowed them to do so.
Can the minister explain, then, why United Kingdom troops are now training in Australia?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that I can explain it, but I have a shrewd idea. There are certain conditions there which are peculiarly suitable for the training of troops in the new weapons of warfare and which do not exist in Canada. May I put it in that way.

There are a few questions I should like to ask the minister, but before I state them I must express strong disagreement with the lack of faith which the hon. member for Lethbridge has in the united nations organization. I will not say much on that question at this time, except to observe that if his view were shared generally, the united nations organization would be bound to fail. If the organization is not successful in developing techniques for

Supply-National Defence
world peace, with all the difficulties involved, then this generation will not know a world worth living in.
The questions I should like to ask the minister are these. In British Columbia we had the Pacific coast militia rangers, a branch of the militia, which I am sure the minister will agree did splendid work. Since the war has ended, members of the Pacific coast militia rangers have formed an incorporated body, and I should like to know whether the minister is considering this and similar organizations as civilian rifle clubs when it comes to granting the benefits which the Department of National Defence has extended to civilian rifle clubs in the past. Again, I notice in Reynolds Neios of London, England, of July 14, that the United States is forming an arctic army of 4,500 officers and men, iwho will be trained in Alaska and in arctic waters. These men will comprise land, sea and air forces. Can the minister tell the committee whether any arrangement has been made for cooperation between the Canadian military authorities and those of the United States with regard to manoeuvres and operations of that type? One other question. Are there going on in the north at the present time any manoeuvres which can be regarded as a summer supplement" to the Musk-Ox exercise?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
At the present time there are no operations which could be considered comparable with Musk-Ox.
On the second question which my hon. friend has raised, as to whether we are cooperating with the Americans in the training of troops, that is a matter which would normally be discussed through the permanent joint board for defence. I shall have to see whether there is anything in that regard, but I doubt whether it would be desirable or necessary to make a public announcement in the house.
As regards the Pacific coast rangers, I will ask my parliamentary assistant to reply. He is more familiar with the question than I am.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The question of the Pacific coast militia rangers has received considerable study by the department. My hon. friend will recall that at the last session there was a-question of permitting the members to retain the rifles which they had used, and that was eventually settled. The question of perpetuating the P.C.M.R. and other similar organizations which were established during the war and providing for the reactivation in time of war is under consideration at the present time as is that of the different rifle clubs and associations which existed before
the war. The question is receiving the active consideration of the general staff at the present time and a solution should be had shortly.

This afternoon I expected that the minister would make a few remarks in reply to the extremely pertinent questions posed by the hon. member for Nanaimo. One of the matters which he dealt with is of such importance that I should like some information on it. I refer particularly to the composition of our permanent force. I have read the newspapers fairly carefully and all that I know about our permanent force has been gleaned from newspaper sources. From that source I gather that it will consist of 25,000 men, and that included in it there will be a brigade group. Apart from that, hon. members and the country generally know practically nothing of it.
The term "a brigade group" is an elastic one. I should like to know what the group is to consist of. On occasions during the past war a division was broken up into brigade groups. Such groups ordinarily consisted of three infantry battalions and their headquarters, a regiment of field artillery, a battery of anti-tank artillery, ack-ack batteries, company engineers, army service corps, a field workshop, field ambulance, along with several other minor odds and ends of various kinds. That was a brigade group. When it was actually performing in a fighting role it ordinarily had attached to it an armoured regiment and sometimes more artillery. I should like the minister to tell us what the brigade group of the permanent force is to consist of. Is. it to be a brigade group such as I have just outlined, which would consist of about 4,500 men, or, with the addition 'of an armoured regiment, about 5,200 men? Is it to consist of a lot more units? That is a matter upon, which we should have further information.
