I should also like the minister to tell us where this brigade group is to get its training; where is it to be concentrated, if it is to be concentrated. When this plan came out first I understand that the brigade group was to be held in one particular spot where it could carry on the training and be available as a striking force to go immediately into action. I believe those were the words by which it was described when we first heard of it. My understanding now is that it is to be split up into units spread all over the country, and quite evidently it is not to be a force which is to be available for immediate action at any time. If you have a brigade group and another group of people spread across Canada and you want to concentrate them for immediate action it will take considerable time.
Supply-National Defence

I know that from experience. These are questions in connection with the brigade group on which we should have some information.
Furthermore, if the brigade group is as large as the one I have described; in other words, if it is to consist of approximately 5,000 men, what is the remainder of the permanent force going to do? Before the war we had an authorized permanent force of 10,000 men. Actually I do not think we had at any time any more than 5,000 men in the permanent force before the war. If you allow 5,000 or
7,000	men for the brigade group it will still leave between 18,000 or 20,000 men in our post-war permanent force. I should like to know what they are to do. From my knowledge I presume generally that part of it will be used in administrative work of various kinds; part of it will be on the staff of national defence headquarters, Canadian military headquarters, and so forth, and part of it will be used to train the reserve army, but it is really not very much good. The reserve army, so far as I can see, is going to be a glorified pre-war non-permanent active militia, as stated by the hon. member for Nanaimo this afternoon, trained, as well as everything else being done, by 5,000 men. I have, as a matter of fact, a shrewd suspicion that a large number of these 18,000 men are to be what I would call wasted away in holding down a whole lot of administrative jobs, which will consist chiefly of men sitting behind desks and signing an innumerable number of forms of various kinds, on the bottom of each the following words will be found "passed to you". It would go to somebody else in the department, and he would also sign the form and pass it on to somebody else.
As one who took a considerable interest in the militia before the war and who is taking a considerable interest in it now, actually I am fearful that that is what will happen to a large number of these 18,000 to 20,000 men who will not be in this brigade group. I should like some clarification of that, and perhaps I shall have a few remarks to make on the matter later.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: With regard to the first part of the hon. member's remarks concerning the composition of the proposed active force, may I say I believe that the information has been given in various press releases. Possibly it did not give all the information which my hon. friend wishes, but he will understand why. This information is of a technical nature and normally would not be given in such releases. However, if my hon. friend desires it I shall be pleased to give him the type of units which it is proposed will form the brigade group to which he has referred.
Is it the type of thing I have just described, or something else?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is a little more detailed than what my hon. friend mentioned. It has been given to the press, as I have already stated. Besides the brigade group headquarters, it will consist of two armoured regiments, three infantry regiments, one artillery regiment, one medium battery, two anti-aircraft batteries, two coast batteries, one anti-tank battery and the various signal sections and troops of a single brigade group. I think my hon. friend knows what I mean when I say "E" section, "X" troop and "Y" troop. There will also be a R.C.A.S.C. infantry brigade group company, one independent brigade ordnance field park, then the various R.C.E.M.E. units, which will go under the heading of the composite brigade workshop, and five various "L.A.D.'s" who serve the units which I have just mentioned. I think my hon. friend will agree that this is information which could not very well be given in a press release, and neither would it interest the general public.
How many men all told?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Approximately 8,000. I am having that figure looked up to give the accurate one.
As regards the remainder of the 25,000 men to which my hon. friend referred as doing practically nothing, may I say that they form part of various static establishments which are dispersed in the various districts and commands, and which are necessary for the maintenance of the brigade group and for the various army schools established throughout the country. For my hon. friend's information, may I say there are thirteen engineer companies, one for each district, and a district signal section for each district. There is also a supply and transport company, R.C.AJ3.C., for each district. Perhaps it will make the position clearer for my hon. friend if I tell him that in each district the following units will exist: a district headquarters; a works company, R.C.E.; district signals; district company, R.C.A.S.C.; district medical company, R.C.A. M.C.; district workshop, R.C.E.M.E.; detachment of the pay corps; detachment of the dental corps, and also personnel of the Canadian provost corps as might be detailed for a provost section in each district. It is also proposed to have schools for the various corps which will compose the brigade group, and I think my hon. friend will agree that all these establishments can very well absorb the remainder of the personnel to which he was referring.

Supply-National Defence
With regard to the brigade group, I now have the figure, which totals 7,259 as being the establishment for the proposed field force.

The brigade group seems essentially the type of brigade group we knew overseas, except that it has two armoured regiments instead of one, as is normal. But there is a terrific anomaly here; it has two coastal batteries. How they are going to pick up these big, heavy coast guns and gallop about the country with them, I do not know.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I gave him the field force, and it includes two coast batteries.

In future, when the
parliamentary assistant is talking about this group, perhaps he would be wise to leave out these coastal batteries, because I can assure him they are extraordinarily difficult to get mobile.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I know that; I am not an expert on the subject, but I have seen them.

Apparently this brigade group is really simply the normal brigade group we became so familiar with overseas during the war, except that it has two armoured regiments instead of one, but that sometimes happened over there as well. It takes in 7,259 men. Apparently the remaining
18,000	men are to be scattered about the country in engineer detachments, signals, army service corps and so on in each military district. We had detachments of all these people in each military district before the war. That is nothing new; that is the same old thing. Probably we are to have more than we had before the war; but the point I am getting at, the thing that struck me in reference to this set-up from the beginning, is that if you have a permanent army of 25,000 men it seems to me the organization and set-up is extraordinarily bad if you have only 7,259 men with whom you can fight. In addition, I should like to know whether these 7,259 men are to be concentrated in a brigade group which might be used as a small striking force, or if they are to be scattered across the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend will quite understand that in the period of organization these various units may be stationed wherever their permanent stations happen to be, without any need to group them together. But it is proposed that this brigade will undergo periods of training as a group.

I still do not think I have had an answer. The parliamentary assistant says they will undergo periods of
training as a group. That is what we did before the war in the non-permanent units which had companies or batteries or whatever it was scattered over quite a section of the country. We were brought together and went to camp to train for seven days; and we did a fair amount of reasonably effective training. But if you are to have a brigade group that is any good at all you must have them together; you must be training them, not for a week or two weeks or three months or some other period some time in the future; they have to be together all the time. The group must be training and working together, particularly if there is any truth in the rumour I have heard that this is intended to be an airborne brigade group. If this brigade group is to remain scattered across the country from Vancouver to Halifax it is not a brigade group at all; it is a few scattered units who are on permanent army pay and, as the hon. member for Nanaimo said this afternoon, are available to put. on demonstrations from time to time, on July 1 and other festive occasions. As a fighting force it is not of much use. I really think the minister should take back this scheme for a Canadian post-war army, take a look at what happened during the last war and what may happen in the future, with the technical advances in warfare which have been taking place, and then bring in something that will do us at least some good. If we had a brigade group that could be a fighting force and that was ready to go some place and do something I would say that would be at least a good start. But if we are to have a so-called brigade group which is scattered all over the country in dribs and drabs and in that position, is no good for anything as far as fighting is concerned, then the government have done nothing and are wasting the money of the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I did not notice in the remarks of my hon. friend any very helpful suggestions. I might point out to him that at the present time the only logical thing to do is to have the units of this brigade group mobilized and recruited in various parts of Canada. I do not think my hon. friend could achieve any good results at this time if he tried to organize that field force or fighting force in one section of Canada. Not only that; as I have told the hon. gentleman, it is proposed that this group will be brought together for collective training. My hon. friend has had personal experience in that type of work. He spent a good deal of time training in England during the last war. He knows that, however you might have been brigaded or in a division, the amount of time any unit spent in actual collective training
Supply-National Defence

as a group, a brigade group or a division, was much limited. Each imit was left to train by itself most of the time, except for special manoeuvres which were part of the collective training, and that is what it is intended to do under the present proposal.

The hon. member for Calgary East mentioned that this brigade group which is being so thoroughly discussed was widely mentioned in. the press as being the nucleus of an airborne group. May I ask the parliamentary assistant or the minister whether it is the intention to make this group into an airborne mobile group?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am informed it is proposed that this group might be trained in airborne operations, and to that end an establishment is being created to permit of possible training in that line.
How does the parliamentary assistant propose to transport this group in airborne operations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I understand the establishment proposes to have a joint training scheme with the R.C.A.F. in Carberry, Manitoba.
Mr; SKEY': That is the answer I expected and the one which, as a matter of fact, I had been seeking.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Why did you not ask right away? We would tell you.

It might interest the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence to know that it requires at least six squadrons of thirty transport aircraft to transport a group of 5,400 men, and that the R.C.A.F. at the present time proposes to have only two squadrons of transport aircraft of a much lesser number than the thirty with which they operated during the war. Therefore all I wish to say is that it is farcial for the Canadian army to develop an airborne group which the Canadian air force cannot carry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think the hon. member wants to be fair, I told him it was intended to train that brigade group -as an airborne group. I believe that for purposes of training it is not quite necessary to have the squadrons to which my hon. friend refers. I quite agree that if this group were called upon to go into action as an airborne group, possibly he would be quite right. But I only said the group would be trained. I am informed that adequate facilities exist to carry out that training.

While we are talking about a brigade group, I should like to ask another question. I was wondering if the parliamentary assistant could translate his delightfully vague statement, the fact that this brigade group will be drawn together for training, into a definite and specific statement as to when it will be drawn together, and if it will then stay together.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is proposed that the group will be brought together summer and winter, and I believe the present localities being considered for such are Wainwright and Borden.
Does the parliamentary assistant mean this coming winter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It will be necessary to get the group together first.

Last session we were slowly winding up the estimates for world war II. These estimates now coming down may very well be the first estimates for world war III. We here this evening are discussing estimates from the point of view of national defence. In other words, a majority in parliament has accepted the principle that national defence is necessary. According to the estimates, we are to get a few more tanks, a few more planes and a few more ships; and we are calling that national defence.
Mark you, this is costing the taxpayers of Canada a great deal of money. But I would look at it from this point of view: Is it national defence, in the light of modern technology? I have before me a clipping from the New York Times magazine of June 23, 1946. This article is by Albert Einstein and states:
Being an ingenious people, Americans find it hard to believe there is no foreseeable defence against atomic bombs. But this is a basic fact. Scientists do not even know of any field, which promises us any hope of adequate defence. The military-minded cling to old methods of thinking-
How true!
-and one army department has been surveying possibilities of going underground, and in war time placing factories in places like Mammoth cave. Others speak of dispersing our population centres into "linear" or "ribbon" cities.
Reasonable men with these new facts to consider refuse to contemplate a future in which our culture would attempt to survive in ribbons or in underground tombs. Neither is there reassurance in proposals to keep a hundred thousand men alert along the coasts scanning the sky with radar. There is no radar defence against the V-2, and should a "defence" be developed after years of research, it is not humanly possible for any defence to be perfect. Should one rocket with atomic warhead strike Minneapolis, that city would look almost exactly

Supply-National Defence
like Nagasaki. Rifle bullets kill men, but atomic bombs kill cities. A tank is a defence against a bullet but there is no defence in science against the weapon which can destroy civilization.
Further to that line of argument I have here a heading from an article appearing in the Saturday Evening Post, of July 13, 1946. The heading states: "Your flesh should creep." The article is by Joseph and Stewart Alsop,' and the head note is as follows:
Did our national safety die at Hiroshima? Can we protect the country against atomic warfare? Experts of the general staff, after calmly studying frightful possibilities, see no military defence-and only one hope. Here are the facts -cold turkey.
In the light of that, I submit that the setting up of a few more tanks or a few more aeroplanes is useless. What you are seeing to-day is the atomic bomb brought into actual warfare. Yet in your selfishness, your fright of modern planning in society, your fear of giving up your little pieces of private property, you are going to wait until the crisis develops; then we shall be catapulted into the war, and the military will take over and do the planning. Democracy will not be allowed to work to bring in a planned order of society.
AVhen that day comes the civilian population will take the rap, and where will your army be? It will be away out somewhere with all the cities and communications cut out behind it. I rather pity the Minister of National Defence in this day and age when he comes to the House of Commons with a defence scheme such as this. It reminds me of the English comedian who describes Harold at the battle of Hastings, when he said, "There sat 'arold, on his 'orse, with 'is eye full of arrer, and 'is axe in 'is 'and." What we are doing has just about as much application to our modern scientific age.
If this nation is to survive this period of war and strife-and seemingly capitalism does produce wars-there is still hope of raising democracy among the people of the world, so that they will be able to stop it in time. But if they do not, we shall get well paid for it. A planned society would plan our cities and plan our life, and we have yet time to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just as in Russia.

That in itself would set the pattern for the rest of the world to follow, because there are other things which stem from a planned society. World trade takes a definite pattern when you operate in a planned society, as we did during the war. We would not be going out trying to cut the other fellow's throat; we would be back on the old lend-lease principle that we had during the war when we were trying to survive, a principle of trade under which we went out to help the other fellow as well as to help ourselves, rather than try to beat the other fellow to it. We know we can expect a depression or a falling off in trade, a struggle for world markets, and so on. Let us not kid ourselves. In the international markets of the world there are two systems competing with each other. There is the barter or bulk sales system, wherein the total state trades with the other states, and there is the method of laissez-faire.
The planned order at the present time has not the majority of governments on its side. But remember this, that it is winning victories among the people. In the backward countries of the world our society has a tendency too often to stay with the old landlord, moneylending classes in those countries. And the revolutionary psychology that comes in and says, "We will redistribute the land among the people", is the one trend influencing the people, with the result that we are losing them.
When we go out to try to establish business relationships we have to use armed force in order to establish trade among those populations. Here on the home front we consider labour as a cost factor in production. Remember this, that the day war breaks cut this time it will be a different set of circumstances. I think it was Hegel, the German philosopher, who said that history repeats itself twice, first as a tragedy and then as a farce. We have had two world wars; look out for the third.
Keyserlingk, who is the managing director of British United Press, points out in an article that there is a boundaryless conflict going on between the communal method of living and the individual method of living. If you want to establish a society in which you can get the support of the people you will have to deal out a great deal more justice at the present time than you are doing. Your total war will not just take on national proportions; it will split society right down the middle, on an international plane, and you will have a class war on your hands. However, if people of good will control any such organization as the united nations we shall not face that catastrophe. But let us not insult our intelligence by calling this national defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have listened with interest and some amusement to the doctrines of the hon. member for Skeena, which are nothing but indoctrinated communism. It is all very well to speak in Canada of a planned society. There has been much done by various administrations toward certain measures for a planned society, but Canada is never going to stand for a system of government
Supply-National Defence

that will drive us into a brutal system of communistic control. We still believe in Canada in a measure of freedom and free enterprise, combined in certain cases, of course, with a measure of control by the orderly processes of government. But as one to whom Canada has been very kind, and as one who has benefited from the orderly processes of democracy in this free and generous land, I must repudiate with all the strength at my command such dangerous doctrines as those just enunciated to this parliament by the hon. member for Skeena.

Several weeks ago the minister said that he would welcome any suggestions that would curtail spending either by the government or by the Department of National Defence. I therefore draw his attention to the Canadian inspection board.
On April 1 of this year the United Kingdom and Canada inspection board ceased to exist, and from then on it carried on as it does now under the name of the Canadian inspection board. From April 1 to July 1 that inspection board cost this country over $600,000. At that rate it will cost Canada this year over $2,500,000.
On that board, as of July 1, 1946, there was a personnel of 1,180, made up of civilian employees, hourly paid, 275; civilian employees, salary paid, 865; seconded service personnel, 36; on loan, not paid by Canada, United Kingdom staff, four. Of that seconded service personnel twenty-six from the army- one major-general, one colonel, five lieutenant-colonels, nine majors, nine captains and one lieutenant. How that one lieutenant got in there I do not know.
He had to do all the work.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He must have been a Liberal.

Besides those, there were air force and navy personnel to bring the total of seconded staff to thirty-six. The breakdown of pay and allowances shows that the pay and allowances for this year increased from $53,688 to $212,000, or an increase of $158,312. My thought is that apparently up to April 1, the United Kingdom were paying the greater part of the shot, but now that the Canadian authorities have taken over, they have reduced the personnel considerably, and those seconded from the army, navy and air force have been reduced in numbers, so that there should be no need for this great increase in pay and allowances.
In addition, this board maintains expensive offices in Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto and

perhaps elsewhere. The board maintains also a laboratory for research work, in spite of the fact that the government has already a research council to do such work.
I come to one branch of this inspection service, that dealing with leather inspection. What leather have they to inspect to-day other than boots? We have no mounted regiments. They were all mechanized during the war. Nor have I heard of any leather upholstery being put in tanks, and even if it were, we are not building any tanks to-day. So that brings us down to boots. I would imagine that we have enough boots in defence stores to-day to last any one of the permanent force sendees for years to come. I suggest that the present inspection staff in the leather branch are on enforced vacation. In Toronto -and I presume the situation is the same in Montreal and other inspectional centres-the staff appear at the office in the morning and, if there is nothing to do, they are told to get out, go home, fade away. That is happening day after day. I urge the minister to go through this inspectional board from top to bottom, and I am sure that, if he does so, he will be able to save this country one million dollars without in any way impairing the efficiency of the organization.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Perhaps I might be
permitted to say a word in answer to the hon. member for Wentworth. The staff of the inspection board has been considerably decreased. I wish to assure the hon. gentleman that that matter is still under review and that further decreases will take place.
As regard the officers of the army and R.C.A.F. who, during the period of the war, were seconded to the inspection board, that matter again is at present being reviewed. If their work is necessary on the board it is proposed that the organization will absorb them and they will cease to be seconded from one of the services.
In a consideration of the requirements for inspection during peace time, it must- be borne in mind that the inspection organization was an integral part of our war production scheme. However, the extent of its activities should not be related solely to the size and requirements of the armed services, nor does the fact that these services are being considerably reduced decrease by so much the activities of the board. In the assignment of duties to the inspection board this has been taken into consideration. But another factor which has been considered is the coordination of inspection facilities with other government departments. Furthermore, in addition to its normal direct inspections, the board is also required to carry

Supply-National Defence
out such development or trial and test work as it may be expedient to allot to it. I can assure the hon. member that such research work

it may be laboratory work-which may be done by the board is not such as is duplicated in the other research establishments, under either the army or national research, but that in fact the creation of the defence research and development sub-department of national defence has in mind the coordination of the research work in order not to permit such duplication to take place.

May I refer the parliamentary assistant to the fact that for the item in connection with machine guns, rifles, et cetera there is no amount required this year, and also that many of these proving grounds where shells and armaments were inspected have been closed down.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is not any item this year for that.
I said that, but I am just answering the parliamentary assistant.

It was not my intention to say anything here, but I am not going to let the Minister of Veterans Affairs get away with calling "communism" when confronted with arguments that he cannot answer. I happen to know the hon. member for Skeena well. I know the hon. member is not a communist, and it is not communism to warn this house that we are living in the age of the atomic bomb; it is not communism to urge that we make full use of the united nations; it is not communism to urge this house that we should plan our affairs so that we shall avoid some of the disasters of the kind we have got into in the past. None of these things is communism.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs says that he is one of those people to whom this democracy has been very good. I, too, am one of those people to whom this democracy has been very good. But there are people in this country to whom this democracy has not been good. That is not necessarily the fault of democracy. There are two kinds of people to be feared: those whom a system has treated too well, and those whom a system has treated badly. One will try to keep a bad system which has been good to them, and the others will try to overthrow a good system which has not been good to them. It is between these two that we have, as intelligent human beings, to try to steer a moderate course. This term "communism" can be used so easily and so flippantly without any meaning. Just about a year ago no less a man than Winston Churchill was calling such a man as Clement
Attlee, the present Prime Minister of Great Britain, a communist, also Herbert Morrison, Ernest Bevin and those other men who to-day are doing yeoman work in the interest of democracy. Intelligent men should speak in intelligent terms at a time as serious as the one in which we are now living.
I want to ask the minister a very short question; will he say for what purpose Canada's post-war defence forces are being designed; to fulfil what purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I can answer that very easily. Canada's post-war defence forces are designed to provide, first, a representative group of all arms of the services. We need them now as a permanent professional trained army. In addition they are to provide a force to train the citizen army, the non-permanent active militia, the reserve army-whatever you want to call it-which has been the basis of Canada's fighting force in two wars and would be the basis of our force in any war we fight in the future, assuming we fight a war with an army, which I take it we would. The purpose of this relatively small force is to provide a small but highly trained and skilled professional force which can be expanded in time of war, primarily to train the citizen soldiers who would have to fight that war. That is about as briefly as I can put it.
Then, I understand, the permanent force is designed for training purposes only and not for the defence of Canada or for an overseas commitment. Is that a correct statement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Well, if-which may God forbid-we should get into a war in the next two or three years they would be available to the extent of their numbers, but obviously a force of eight or nine thousand troops together with training cadres and administrative personnel would not have any perceptible effect in any war that we can contemplate. So that I think we must look upon our permanent force as a small, highly trained unit to perform the functions which I have mentioned. Obviously, if our commitments under the united nations call for something more than appears to be now indicated we may have to reconsider our plans, but I think it is fair to say that we should try to make our policy as flexible as possible in order to meet changed conditions with respect to the type of armed forces that are needed, with respect to new weapons, or whatever it may be. There is nothing static about the thing. I do not think I can answer my hon. friend's question more directly.
Supply-National Defence
The minister in answering my question need not have any heat in his voice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did not intend to put any heat into it.
My question was directed, entirely without any guile, to get some information which was not in any of the press releases.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did not intend any heat; I may have been a little more forcible than was required.

Then I suggest to the committee that the minister's answer leaves open, as I thought it would, the whole question of the defence of Canada, and that we should not consider that these forces are in any way adequate or even designed to defend Canada in case her borders were attacked.
I want now to go on to another question. I have here two reports, dated May 17, with respect to proposed standardization of equipment with the United States, and in these press reports it is stated from "official circles" that a programme is under discussion between the Canadian government and the United States government for the standardization of equipment of the armies of the two countries and for coordination of training methods and military organization and a joint erection and staffing of defence and weather stations in the continental arctic zones. Would the minister make a statement as to whether or not there is any truth in this report, and if there is, what progress has been made toward such standardization?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that I have seen the particular report to which my. hon. friend refers. I know there have been a number of reports relating to the standardization of equipment between our armed forces and those of the United States and also those of the United Kingdom, and I know there was a group of' officers and civilians from the United Kingdom out here some months ago who were looking over the field. I am sure there have been no definite decisions taken as to standardization of equipment. As I think I have said on other occasions, it is an end which we in Canada are extremely keen on; we should like to see it.
It is most desirable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is most desirable. We should like to see, so far as it may be practicable, standardization of equipment between our forces, those of our neighbour to the south, and those of the other members of the com-
CMr. Abbott.]
mionwealth. Naturally, as a junior partner we are not in a position to initiate such a move, but we can do everything in our power to encourage it, and1 that is what we intended to do. Considerable headway has been made along those lines. I cannot conceive of any war we would be fighting in which Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States would be fighting on opposite sides, and therefore it is pretty self-evident that we all have an interest in standardizing equipment as far as possible in order that the industrial potential of our countries can be available one to another.

I entirely agree, of course, with the policy of standardization, but I should like the minister to tell the committee if he can, what is in the mind of the government as to high policy in this connection. Is it proposed to standardize on a commonwealth-United States basis or upon a Canada-United States basis, or would both methods be used? Is there any decision on the policy level with respect to that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that I can add very much to what I have already said. Both the United States and the United Kingdom are studying the matter now and we are studying it with them. There is nothing I can add to that.

My next question relates to the Canada-United States defence board. I understand that we have a military mission in Washington, a considerable establishment in London, and of course we have our own chief of staff here. In addition, there is the United States-Canada joint defence board which was set up during the war. Would the minister state how that board fits into the other activities which presumably are carried on separately from the actual board itself; that is, the activities of the mission in Washington and C.M.H.Q. and the more normal forms of liaison between countries?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I will see if I can answer that, not in complete detail but in broad general terms. Canadian military headquarters in London is purely a wartime organization which is being rapidly run down and should be pretty well cleaned up by the end of the year. Just what our permanent arrangements will be in London, I am not yet in a position to say. Normal arrangements, as my hon. friend knows, with other countries are to have our military attaches with the embassy or diplomatic mission. They would ordinarily look after our military interests in a foreign country. In the United Kingdom the military staff would ordinarily be attached to the high commissioner's office. In the United

Supply-National Defence
States, in Washington, since some time early in the war, we have maintained a joint staff mission which has had representatives of the three services. That has been in addition to the ordinary military attache staff at our embassy in Washington. It is proposed to continue that mission for a time at any rate, because it was found extremely useful during the war. It can handle matters rather more easily than can be done through the usual diplomatic channels. Just what the final size of the joint staff mission in Washington will be, I am not yet in a position to say. It is, however, being substantially reduced from what it was during the war. My idea -would be that if it is continued as a permanent feature we should have one top man, a senior officer who might alternate between the three different services. At one lime we might have a senior officer from the army, and then from the navy and then from the air force, with appropriate subordinates in the other services. The permanent joint board, as the committee knows, was set up on August 17. 1940. in order to advise the respective governments with regard to joint plans for the defence of this continent. It was created, as its name implies, to be a permanent joint board of defence, following a discussion between the late President Roosevelt and the Prime Minister (Mr. King), and the thought would be that it will continue as a permanent instrument for an exchange of views between the two countries, to advise the respective governments with respect to the defence of this continent. It is an advisory body pure and simple; it does not determine matters of policy. It is composed of men who have experience in military matters, experts in that line, capable of advising their respective governments, but it is not a policymaking body. From my own limited experience it seems to me it has performed a useful and necessary function and I would hope, and I believe, it will continue to do so in the future.

I wish now to turn to an entirely different subject, and that is the question of the non-permanent militia or rather the reserve army. Any information I have is to the effect that the reserve army is not getting men at the present time and that it is becoming very difficult for some units to keep up any kind of interest or esprit de corps with a slate of -officers and practically no men. It appears to me-and that was really why I asked the original question as to the future purpose of the armed forces of Canada, what purpose they were designed to fulfil-'that the most important thing the .minister could do to help the reserve army come up to strength, apart from what I asked him to do this afternoon about going around drumming up some recruits for us, would be to make an over-all and public statement as to the role of Canada's reserve army in the future years.
The hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out this afternoon how that role might quite easily have changed from one of a force which would provide an- overseas striking force to a force designed to defend the confines of our own country against an aggressor. It is my view that the hon. member for Nanaimo is very likely right and that is the real role of our reserve army, which the minister properly said is our chief bulwark of defence. It seems to me that if that statement were made it would have a very good effect in bringing men to join up in the reserve army. But so long as they do not know exactly why they are in the force, or are invited to join it, and- so long as no one has asked them in Canada's name so to do, I feel that we may easity go along as we did in the first ten years after the last war.
I well remember joining the militia myself in 1929, and I like to think we were a fairly good unit. Yet there was a total of thirty men in the company to which I was posted, of whom fifteen men paraded, and that was ten years after the war. We increased that very-much indeed in the next ten years when these young Canadians had a consciousness that there was a job ahead of them. I am quite sure that statement of the basic purpose of the reserve army and of -the training policy which would be followed would do wonders to build up the kind of reserve army of which the keen officers who have taken up reserve army duty are thinking.
Assuming that by his one-man recruiting campaign and statement of policy the minister recruits these men, how are we to keep them in the militia? I have had considerable experience with that, a very happy experience in one way and an unhappy one in the other. It was a happy experience in the chaps I met, even though they were few, and the mutual interest we had in our unit, and a very unhappy one in the support given by the government to the effort which was being made by the officers and men in the reserve army.
What we needed more than anything else was, of course, the sinews of war, the money To keep a man in the reserve army you must pay him. He must have his pay. Before the war, as the minister knows, we just handed it over to the regimental fund to pay for the light in the armoury on the extra night in the week that we paraded. We were allowed to put on our lights one night in the week. If we wanted to use them for two nights the
Supply-National Defence

men put up their pay for it and for other barrack purposes. I think it might be a good idea, if it could be arranged, that men training in the reserve army be paid a day's pay for each parade, and be paid perhaps more frequently than the way we got it before the war, which was once a year. Of course we never saw it; the exceptional time we did see it we blew it in all at once. It would be a great advantage to the men to know they would get that cash periodically. It would be a splendid way of helping the officers to keep the turnout on parade up to scratch during the training season.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It cost every officer lots of money in the old militia days.

The minister is indeed right; it cost every officer a considerable sum out of his own pocket. I was not making much money and therefore I did not pay much out, but I paid out much more than I could afford.
The next important thing is to provide the men with training equipment. In an infantry battalion before the war we had six Lewis guns. The rifles, such as we had, were not allowed out of the armoury. They were filled up with grease. No man could ever learn how to look after his rifle because he was not allowed to look after it. Further than that, there were not enough to go round. We have now all sorts of much more modern training equipment. I hold in my hand a newspaper clipping. I follow the minister from Cornwall to Ottawa and to the other places where he gives these press releases.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It was a speech I made at Cornwall, not a press release.

It suggested that only fifty per cent of the reserve army will be recruited and that apparently equipment will be provided for only fifty per cent in the case of the infantry; and in the case of the artillery and armoured regiments only thirty-three per cent of the equipment will be provided. I take it, from the fact that we are having only fifty per cent of the' men, that they will get only thirty-three per cent of the fifty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What is my hon. friend quoting from?

I am quoting from an Ottawa press release dated April 16. If I am not making myself clear I shall read it. It
says:
About 50 per cent of the reserve force will be recruited so equipment will be provided for
90,000	troops during the initial period of organization.
[Mrr. Merritt.]
The reserve force infantry will be armed with 100 per cent of its equipment; the artillery and motors 33J per cent; field and medium artillery, 50 per cent; anti-aircraft artillery, 25 per cent; armoured fighting vehicles, a small scale of tanks and self-propelled guns.
I suggest to the minister that this year, if ever, is the time for a more generous scale of equipment for training purposes to be provided to these units. I think he knows and I know that when we get rid of the demobilization vote in these estimates there will not be as much money available for the armed forces as there is this year. It seems to me that when you take into consideration wear and tear and breakages in training the thing to insist on for the reserve army is a much higher percentage of equipment than thirty-three per cent of fifty per cent. I assure the minister that in a reserve army the presence of training equipment is the thing that makes the training go. When you are doing it as regular soldiers you cannot improvise and imagine everything, and with a Monday-night soldier it becomes altogether too difficult. If you do not have the equipment the simple answer is that you do not train in that particular arm. The probability is that the battalion does ceremonial drill where you otherwise might be doing training on one of the weapons.
The next suggestion I wish to make is that the time element is important in the training of a militia unit. You have two or three hours one night a week in which to do all your training.- In that time you must have an inspection and roll-call and do a certain amount of administrative work. In the cities the armouries are downtown and the facilities for training outside the four walls of the armoury are indeed limited. I suggest to the minister that, as an aid to the training of the reserve army and to make the training more interesting there should be in each city certainly, and possibly in many towns, a troopcarrying company R.C.A.S.C., as a permanent part of the active or reserve army, which would be available to lift the unit which wants to go out of its armoury to train in the field. Thus it could do so in its training time and not be forced by lack of mobility to sit around in the armoury. I am sure that the men would respond and find their parades much more interesting and useful to them if they could take advantage of the outdoors to get some of their training and not have to wait, as they did before the war, until the summer camps to do their outdoor training. They never had a chance to do it at all in the winter.
The last matter that I want to bring to the attention of the minister has also to do

Supply-National Defence
with keeping the men interested in the reserve army. I refer particularly to another means of transportation, namely boots. Before the war we had a very difficult experience with our boots. In depression times the men were wearing out shoe leather. We went to our camps in low shoes and all sorts of absolutely ill-suited footwear. It was a great tribute to the men that they ever managed to last out one of these camps with the kind of thing that they had on their feet. There was no free issue of boots by the Department of Natibnal Defence. I ask the minister not to hesitate to give a pair of boots to a man who joins the militia. The officers will look after getting his kit in if he tries to run away with them and does not attend parades. They have always done that with his other kit; and a free issue of boots with no reservation would be a wonderful thing for the reserve army.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend to say that I commenced that policy before the war, the free issue of boots.
Did you ever get them?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
On repayment?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

I have no recollection
of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think it was in 1938.

I am afraid it was not
started quite early enough to come within my experience. This business of boots is a very homely subject, but there is nothing more important to a reserve army soldier. I want to conclude by telling the minister of the difficulties we had in the first three months after mobilization. Because there were no boots for the militia there were no boots for the active army. The particular battalion of which I was a member went overseas in December, 1939, and of course we had trained from September 1. We got our battle dress and our boots about one week before we went overseas. In the meantime we had to excuse men from parade, men who were keen and wanted to parade, because they were literally walking around in their bare feet, with only the uppers of their boots still in working order; and none were available from ordnance stores. Of course that is another reason why the reserve army should have boots during peace time.
Just to sum up, I am certain the minister will get a fine reserve army, which he has not now because he has not the men coming in,
if he declares thie purpose and policy of the reserve army and provides pay, training equipment, transport and boots. If he just looks after those five things I think he will have very great success; if he does not I am sure he will not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard for what he has said about the reserve army; and I thank him also for the suggestions he has made, all of which are most definitely constructive. With him, I do not think we can over emphasize the important role the reserve army, the non-permanent active militia, plays in the military set-up of Canada. As I said a little earlier, it has been the backbone of our fighting force in two wars, and I cannot contemplate any future war in which it would not carry out a similar role. The young men, officers and other ranks, who give of their time and energy in training with the reserve army are rendering a real form of public service. I am glad he has brought that point forward, because it enables me to add emphasis to what has already been said.
We are going to try to make service in the reserve army more attractive than it was before the war. Rates of pay will be the same as those for the active force which, as the committee knows, have been increased. We now have available ample supplies of what to-day is modern equipment. It may not be modern a year or two years or three years from now, but it is modem to-day. We are not so fortunate with respect to accommodation. I realize that in a great many centres there are not suitable quarters for reserve army units, and it is difficult to ask men to turn out and train when they are not furnished with the proper surroundings in which to do so. At the moment we cannot do very much about that, because with the existing shortage of labour and materials it just is not possible to do very much to add to existing facilities in that respect. That handicaps us, too, on this question of equipment. One of our most serious difficulties to-day is to provide suitable storage space for the very large quantity of mechanized and motorized equipment used in a modern unit; and we have that difficulty all over the country. That is one reason, among others, why it is not possible to issue full equipment according to the establishment for all reserve army units, because in a great many cases there is simply no place to store it.
I do not know that I can comment in detail on the other points raised by my hon. friend. As I say, I think all the suggestions he has made are decidedly of a constructive
Supply-National Defence

nature, and I can assure him they will be given careful consideration both by myself and by the officers of my department.

I am not so unwise as to attempt, in the presence of so many distinguished soldiers, to discuss the technical aspects of a defence force. But I do consider myself competent to say a few words about the problems relating to personnel; and on that account I am grateful to the honourable and gallant member who has just spoken for bringing the discussion back from the stratosphere to the -man who wears the boots. In what the hon. member said to the minister he wisely emphasized the importance of maintaining interest and esprit de corps in the army which he called the Monday-night army. We used to call it the Friday-night army; but it is the same army, the chaps who come out once a week.
At the moment it is true, as it was true after the last war and as it will be for some little time yet, that much of the glamour is gone from the uniform, so far as those who have seen actual service and those who are older members are concerned. But if the scheme -which has been outlined is to succeed in the future we shall depend eventually, and very quickly, upon the chaps who are now fourteen or fifteen years of age, in whom we must develop an interest in the non-permanent militia, or whatever it may be called, so that they will seek to join it. Those who have had some experience will realize the importance of boots, the importance of being properly shod. Those who have had the experience of being improperly shod will never forget it. In my judgment it is absolutely true that it is necessary to offer the young fellows of this generation, as it would have been -wise with a previous generation, the inducement of pay to make it possible and profitable for them to sacrifice their leisure time in training.
There is, however, something else. I do not think it is any accident, and certainly the fact has some significance for me-I believe it is a fact-that the first or second regiment to be mobilized in each district at the outbreak of war was a kilted regiment. When the Minister of Veterans Affairs rose to take part in this discussion this evening I thought, "Here it comes," but he got off on another tack and did not mention one of -the most important morale building features of the army. A little later another Scotsman, the hon. member for Vancouver East, took part in the discussion. Again I thought, "Here it comes," but he too forsook the argument I am about to make and with which I am sure both those hon. gentlemen will heartily agree. I refer, of course, to the restoration of the

kilt. For centuries almost, the British army, under the influence of the Irish or sometimes of the Sassenach himself, attempted to abolish the kilt. It is true that during a period of the war they did succeed in getting the soldiers into these battle rompers for purposes of uniformity and for other well established reasons. At this moment I am not going to say anything about the use of battle dress under service conditions, but certainly there is no condition of training which will equal or supersede the experiences which members of the kilted regiments, not only in the British isles but in this country, have been able to endure. If you are to attract the youth of the country into the permanent forces as well as the non-permanent forces you must make * the conditions of service attractive.
Something was said about the kilt this afternoon, and I was reminded of a circumstance in connection with one of the kilted regiments in the city from which the minister himself comes. I was there at the time; I know something about it. It was almost impossible for a Canadian of Scottish descent to get into that regiment, because there was a line-up of volunteers blocks long, composed of French-Canadians, Irishmen, and compatriots of that gallant Scotsman, from Windsor who now represents Spadina in this house. The popularity of the kilt is beyond question. If anyone needs any further indication of that I would refer him to the record of the regiment whose uniform I have had the honour of. wearing, although I never had an opportunity to fight w-ith them. When they lost the kilt in Canada, and were put in what they used to call battle rompers, and were sent to England, the first thing that the rank and file of the regiment did when they got to England was to buy out of their store of money which, as everyone knows, w'as none too plentiful, sometimes at outrageous prices, a kilt, to w-ear when they went on their first leave.
There is something about the kilt which appeals to those with Scottish blood in their veins, which others profess to laugh at, which most admire, and which nearly everyone tries to crawl into whenever Highland regiments are open for enlistments.
I spoke about this matter at the close of the last session, when the minister said to me-very graciously, I thought, but not very satisfactorily-that the Highland regiments would be permitted to wear the kilt when they were -walking out. Since when has the descendant of a highlander, or anyone acting in his name, been "permitted" to wrear the kilt?
I do not make these remarks with any intention of being flippant or of amusing the com-

Supply-National Defence
mittee. but rather to discuss a point which has been brought to my attention by representatives from a considerable number of kilted regiments in Canada. I think I can promise the minister prolonged, serious, repeated, possibly I should say endless raids on his time and patience until there is some recognition of the desire of Canadian youth, whether they be of Scottish descent or not, to wear what is traditionally the costume of fighting men.
I think one of the things that happened in Canada was that when we dismounted the cavalry we remounted too many of them on swivel chairs in. various positions of authority. While I admit the distinction with which they served-and without spurs, in those places-I think they lost something of their appreciation for the traditional garment of fighting men.
Therefore I am not happy about the suggestion which has been made that they are going to continue to issue the kilt to the bands, and to permit the officers and other ranks to wear it while walking out. I know, from my experience and observation in the past, which of the cadet corps in the various centres were the most quickly brought up to strength. I know which regiments were, leaders in most of the districts of Canada, in the period immediately preceding the war. I know the ones which were high in their rating of proficiency, partly because they often had the greatest numbers. The reason they had those members was not unconnected with the historical privilege of wearing the kilt.
To the minister and' his parliamentary assistant I would say that this is a warning of things to come. This matter will come up again and again and again, until you take those battle trousers away from the Highland regiments in Canada, and begin again to issue traditional dress. I speak, not threateningly, but as a promise. With all his undoubted ability and popularity, I am quite sure that the present minister or whoever may eventually succeed him will not succeed in downing this request.
There is one other matter which I think is important to training; perhaps I should say there are two things. The first is to sustain interest. One of the things which killed interest in nearly every non-permanent militia regiment or battery, or whatever it was, in the time between the two wars, was the lack of material with which, to work, and a lack of changing and constantly modernized manuals of training. It did not take the bright lad who was interested in his unit very long to learn as much or more than his instructor, when the only things taught were those which
were in the book. Consequently I point out the importance and the urgency of a constantly changing manual of training.
That leads to the other point, namely a constantly alert and constantly brought up to date instructional cadre. We have laid a great deal of emphasis upon formal education, sometimes unfortunately upon social connections, in the selection of officers and, in fact, the selection of rank and file in the permanent service. Someone has suggested that we have set the educational standards too high. I do not know whether that is so or not. They are idealistic. I should think that if we are to get the numbers we want we may have to reduce them to some extent. But there is one place I hope the minister will not reduce the requirements; that is, in this cadre. If we are to make of casual training something with a continuing interest-and reserve army training has to be casual-we must have good instructors. At the non-commissioned level we should have boy leader types, scout leader types, with instructional ability. I may be setting a high standard, but when a young soldier reaches the point where, with justification, he knows that he knows the score as well as the man whose official position it is to teach him, he may become dissatisfied, lose interest and quit. So that we must provide men who can keep ahead of these lads, or we will lose the interest of those who are there to learn. When you lose their interest, you lose them.

I will not take long, because I have not worn the kilt since I was nine years of age. I agree with what the previous speaker has said. We must not curtail the length of the kilt. After having listened for what seemed like about an hour and a half I wish to tell the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that if he follows out and models his future army after the 29th battalion, which won the last war, he will have sufficient reserves to carry him along.

Mr. Chairman-
Mr. MACKENZIE; Here come the Irish.

I have been informed that in speaking this afternoon the minister made some reference to my calling senior officers at headquarters brass hats. If he will read the speech I made in the house recently he will find that I did nothing of the kind. If he will look at the remarks I made last fall he will see that I had a good word to say for them.
However, my reason for bringing up the question of officers and senior officers was that in my opinion there was a surplus of senior
Supply-National Defence

officers in the services. I think it is the duty of the minister at this time to curtail expenditures and to get down to normalcy as soon as possible.
Something has been said regarding commands. Five new commands have been set up. There are eleven district commands, and another one has recently been established at Whitehorse. It is my opinion that since parliament is going to vote money to have a permanent force and interim army of 25,000 officers and men, we shall find that a great proportion of them, instead of training in the field, will be carrying on jobs in offices, with the result that the actual training force will be limited,
I should like to speak with respect to some aspects of training. I was at Whitehorse recently, and I found that the Royal Canadian Air Force signals had taken over the signal services from the United States army, whereas the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals had, during the years prior to the war and during the war, carried on the signals services in the northwest, and had given good service to the people of that community. If there is to be a signal service in the northwest it should be run by one of the services. You can go right down the line and find duplication of services all along. One thing the minister should set himself to do is to cut out duplication wherever it exists. For example, are there to be headquarters for the three services in the city of Toronto, M.D.2, and the same throughout Canada? If so, it means that we shall have thirty-three district officers commanding the three services throughout Canada and a corresponding number of headquarters. It does seem to me-and I am sure that the hon. member for Nanaimo must have brought this up-that the commands are likely to get top-heavy. I should like the minister to look into that at the first opportunity.
I come now to the question of Whitehorse.
I do not know what commitments Canada made regarding the maintenance of the Alaska highway. But there is a very small force of men in Whitehorse and, if that small detachment of men is to maintain the highway, it will not be long before it gets into disrepair. If we have to maintain that highway, that section of the country offers great opportunity for the training of engineers in bridge-building, roadwork and many other types of experience which they cannot get in eastern Canada. It is a great potential training ground, not so much for infantry as for the outside engineering services. I do not know what latitude is allowed to the officer commanding in Whitehorse, but I know a number of men in Whiter horse desired to get back into the service and

they were told that they could not get back unless they were first sent to Calgary to take their basic training. The idea of sending them to Calgary for basic training, after they have been several years in the army, seemed to me a little stupid. I wonder whether the minister is going to carry on all these senior officers in defence headquarters as well as the districts- deputy ministers of this and that, holding the rank of major and brigadier?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No deputy minister holds that rank.
Every deputy minister is a brigadier, to the best of my knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not one of them.
Then you must have replaced them in the last few days.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They have never held that rank.
I meant deputy branch heads, not deputy ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No; all directors are colonels.

That is fine. Would the minister give us a list of the commitments for $25,843,524 mentioned in the item? The reason I ask is that the hon. member for Wentworth brought up this evening the question of the Canadian inspection board, and I am wondering why 1,180 men should be kept on the strength of the board to look after a small number of contracts. Will the minister give us a list of the items?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Answering some of my hon. friend's other points first, I know he paid a visit to Whitehorse and had an opportunity of meeting at first hand some of our personnel on the Alaska highway. In April of last year it became necessary for the Canadian government to take over the Alaska highway, the northwest staging route, the air fields on the way to Alaska and the land lines providing communication with those air fields. There was no organization capable of taking on the Alaska highway other than the Canadian army, and the army agreed to take it over. We have set up special facilities, engineering units, to do that work, which is under the direction of Brigadier Walsh, a capable permanent force engineer officer, and, by the way, a graduate of McGill, which is in his favour. The air force naturally took over the northwest staging route and the maintenance of the air fields. The land lines were the means of communication between those air fields, and the air force took them on too. That required a considerable number of technical personnel, details of which my colleague the Minister of National

Supply-National Defence
Defence for Air would be in a position to give. It was no easy task for the air force to take on. They were not anxious to do it. They do not want it now and they are keen to turn it over to a civilian agency as soon as possible. The same applies to the Alaska highway, although we are glad to get experience there for our engineers.
I did not suggest that the highway be turned over to a civilian agency, but that it would be a good training ground for the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals, operating in the northwest territories.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The Royal Canadian Corps of Signals continues to operate in that district, but we have not the personnel to operate the specialized job of handling the land lines between the aerodromes.
As to the inspection board, I do not know whether my hon. friend was in his seat when my parliamentary assistant gave some information about the work the board is now carrying on. May I add to what he said the general statement that the staff is being reduced and will continue to be reduced just as quickly as possible. But, as the committee will appreciate, we still have some 45,000 to 50,000 men in the services and they require considerable quantities of material. There are also a considerable number of contracts outstanding on which inspection work has to be done. But I am satisfied the staff will decrease pretty rapidly.

I feel that this
would be an opportunity under this general item to secure some information that I found some difficulty in the last few days in being able to secure. The matter has become almost an impenetrable wall of m3rstery. I am sure that the Minister of National Defence will be able to furnish at least a portion of the information that I have been trying to secure. It has to do with a matter that I have been asking questions about, connected with certain army rejections or medical discharges which allegedly were signed in blank by Major J. A. Elliott, A19, R.C.A.S.C., at Camp Borden. In the return that was brought down, the answer given by the Department of National Defence was that this matter would be fully covered by the correspondence which would be brought down by the Department of Justice, and the Department of Labour furnished the same answer.
To begin at the beginning, possibly I can secure from the minister a report on any investigation that took place in the army in connection with these army rejections or
medical discharges and also what disposition, if any, was made of Major Elliott as a result of the investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to ask my hon. friend to allow that question to stand for a few minutes because I have not the information here at the moment. I am advised that all the correspondence in the Department of National Defence was produced. I have no, report here as to what happened to Major Elliott. I can probably give my hon. friend an answer a little later this evening.

I want to say one thing to the minister with regard to the reserve army, or militia, or whatever name it is to go by in the future. I ask him not only to give the civilian soldiers an opportunity to have, to handle and to use the weapons which are considered modern at the present time, but, as new weapons are invented and manufactured, to allow the reserve army to have those new weapons. I say this with a particular experience in mind. A week after the fall of Dunkirk, and later, I was training with an N.P.A.M. and at Niagara camp, and we did not have any rifles which would fire. By a stroke of good fortune, the D.O.C., M.D. 2, at that time was able to get some new rifles, or at least he thought they were new; they were in their original cases; and the morale and enthusiasm of the entire battalion grew at a tremendous pace, until we opened the boxes containing those rifles and found that they were Ross rifles Mark II, or perhaps Mark III; anyway they had been declared obsolete and useless in 1917. But all the same they were "new" rifles. I have never seen anything which destroyed the morale of a unit so much. Admittedly they were new rifles, but we expected something quite different; what we got were Ross rifles made as far back as 1915, or perhaps 1914. At that time, after the fall of Dunkirk, the entire camp expected an invasion of the United Kingdom; and nothing could have damaged the morale of the troops more than the kind of weapons which we had in the year 1940.
So I say to the minister, no matter what new weapons are invented, let your civilian soldiers see them and use them. If there is another war it will be your civilian soldiers who will fight it. That has always been so in our history. We are not a country of great standing armies; we never can be; we are a country of civilian soldiers. So through you, Mr. Chairman, I ask the minister, on behalf of these civilian soldiers who train one day a week, please give them an opportunity to use the new weapons. If there is a war, they will have to fight it. Do not supply them with old Ross rifles or the weapons of the
Supply-National Defence

Crimean war; give them an opportunity to use jet weapons, and, as the new science of atomics expands, let them, if possible, see the weapons it produces and use them. Do not condition your thinking as of the year 1945, when the last war ended. New weapons are being constantly invented, and it is a peculiarity of the human race that they will continue to be invented and will become more deadly and devastating as time goes on. Let your civilian army see these weapons and train with them.
Do not treat your reserve army as something that goes to camp for a holiday for two weeks in every year. Do not treat the camp as a social attribute or a social function. Your reserve army in the next war will require to be far more efficient than it has ever been before, and the men of the reserve army must have a degree of knowledge of modern weapons, the weapons which may be produced in 1948, 1949, 1950. You cannot all of a sudden start to teach them the use of jet weapons if they have had nothing but impulse weapons to train with. I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, that unless that is done the training of the reserve army will be largely wasted.
The science of warfare is moving at a constantly accelerated pace. We cannot afford to take another chance. If there should be a third world war we shall not have months, perhaps not even weeks, to prepare. Your civilian army must be trained; it must be keen; it must know the weapons or the prototypes of the weapons with which they will have to do the fighting. I ask the Minister of National Defence not to allow the reserve army of the next few years to degenerate,-I will not say "degenerate", but "deteriorate"-because	there was nothing
degenerate in the old N.P.A.M.; it was a fine force, but it did not have weapons. Nor did it have boots; at least my battalion did not have boots. We helped to provide them with boots, and for years the officers paid money to take them to camp. Do not ever let us get into that state again. Let us never again lower the guard of this country, for the enemy will be more vicious than man; the weapons will be more terrible than any we have yet seen. I say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister and to his staff, particularly the director of military training, keep up your training of the reserve army; give them modern weapons; see to it that they are kept keen, and also see to it that being a member of the reserve army is not a social function but a patriotic job, a job as indis-

pensatole to the safeguarding and security of this country as the highest of our democractic processes.

There is a matter in connection with the selection of officers for the permanent army on which I should like to ask the minister a few questions. My information, as well as my experience, is that a certain amount of dissatisfaction exists among men who served overseas as officers, and there is a widespread feeling among them that there have been appointed as officers in the permanent army a considerable number of men who had no service except in Canada or in England; in other words, that quite a number of officers of the permanent army are men who had no actual battle experience and did no fighting. They have been appointed to the detriment of men who actually did fight overseas. I took up with the minister two cases which he will remember. Both of these men had special qualifications; both had applied for the permanent force, and both had been turned down on the question of age. One man was about a year over age and the other, nearly two years. I understand that a considerable number of officers who rose from the ranks and who did extremely well in the army overseas have been turned down for admittance to the permanent force as officers.
In this connection, I should like to point out thht some of these men, while they may be a little over age, while in some cases their educational requirements may not be up to the standards now demanded, have a large degree of technical knowledge which I know personally it would be absolutely impossible for any man to obtain under peacetime conditions. One of these men to whom I refer served as technical adjutant of S.P., an artillery regiment, which is essentially an armoured regiment equipped with tanks. He was one of five or six such men in the army, and in virtue of his job he acquired a vast amount of technical knowledge which it is extremely difficult for any man to get, and more or less impossible unless he gets it under active service conditions. One of the men turned down for a commission was this very man I have in mind.
I do not care whether the national defence headquarters gets a man who passed with honours in mathematics or in any subject in a university and then trains him for four years afterwards, he will not be as good a man on that particular job as the type of technical man about whom I have spoken. It is a great pity, therefore, that this policy is being pursued. In connection with it I would ask a few questions. I thiDk the minister has

Supply-National Defence
