this case in mind, because I wrote to him with reference to it and intimated that I would ask some questions regarding it under the estimates. First, how many officers have been accepted for the permanent army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The number was 2,027 as at August 8.
Second, how many of these have had service in Canada only?

Perhaps I can break that down. The number who servedi in theatres of operations was 1,140; the number who served in England for a year or more, 259; the number who served in England for less than a year but over sixty days, 295; and the number who served in Canada only, 333.
I take it that out of the 2,027, 1,140 had actual fighting experience; in other words, about half. How many of these officers have had merely what we call a Cook's tour in the actual fighting area?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: None of these.
And how many in actual fighting formations? Does the minister say none had merely the so-called Cook's tour?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.
My information is that a little more than half of the officers so far accepted have had actual fighting experience, and 240-is that the number?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: 333 served in Canada only.

There were 333 who served in Canada only. I submit that when we finished the war we had the finest young men in Canada in our fighting forces, the majority of them at any rate having served overseas, and it is a serious lapse on the part of the Department of National Defence army that only half the officers had fighting experience, or little more than half, while 333 never left the shores of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A good many of those are specialists, R.C.E.M.E. staff and that sort of thing.

I have already mentioned, however, that quite a number of highly trained specialists, men who gained knowledge by virtue of battle experience which cannot be obtained otherwise, are the very men who are being turned down. This afternoon the hon. member for Kingston City spoke of certain officers, and I have no brief as far as that particular matter is concerned, but the minister at that time made an interjection and said, "We are trying to build an efficient army". I was glad to hear that, but when I learned that upwards of half of the officers 63260-319
accepted in the permanent force had no fighting experience, while a considerable number never went outside Canada, whereas on the other hand men with a wealth of fighting experience, men who demonstrated their work, are being refused, then I say that the minister is not giving any evidence that the department is trying to build an efficient army in regard to the reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I will reply to my hon.
friend briefly. As I said this afternoon, I do not personally select the officers in the army and it would be improper besides being impassible for me to do so. There is a selection committee in which I have confidence, who carefully review all applications for commissioned ranks in the post-war permanent force. I may say we have a great many applications, something over 6,000 already, and up to August 8 there have been 2,395 accepted. These have to cover all categories, all age groups, all types of service. So far as I have been able to ascertain, the selection committee is doing a careful, conscientious job in endeavouring to select the most competent officers for the post-war permanent force. That is all I can say. Lines of policy are laid down. Overseas service and operational experience are very much in a man's favour;, nevertheless those are not the only qualifications, and I hope and believe that we shall have a competent, highly skilled officer corps in the post-war army.
How many are graduates from the military college, and how many have risen from the ranks?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not that information but I could get it. A very small .proportion would be graduates of the military college because it has been closed since 1940 or 1941, and out of the total of 2,395, I would think a comparatively small number were graduates of the military college. If I may hazard a guess, I believe a substantial number would be men who had started in the ranks. As I say, however, I am only offering a guess because I have not the figure.
May I interrupt to say that even those who were in the military college rose from the ranks, and they were fairly severe ranks too.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am aware of that.

What are the regulations in regard to the use of army vehicles by personnel and those workers employed by the army? What I am getting at is this. In Ottawa as well as in other parts of the country

Supply-National Defence

army vehicles have been used for personal purposes. Here in Ottawa, I know of a couple of cases where army trucks were used to take furniture from a home in this city out to a summer cottage, and they have been used to cart stuff from one place to another, even beer to a man's home.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to have a case of that kind brought to my attention, because it is strictly contrary to the regulations. Every time we find out about it we take appropriate action.
I have cases here that I shall let the minister have.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad if my hon. friend will let me know about them.

I had correspondence with the minister in regard to an army vehicle smashing into a civilian car. If these cars or trucks are being used for civilian purposes, or not authorized to be used, the minister's department can say: "The use of this truck or vehicle was not authorized by the department and therefore the department is not liable for any damage." The minister said in a letter to me, dated July 5, regarding an accident:
A very thorough review of the facts and circumstances surrounding the accident involving the accident to Mr. Long has now been made. It appears that the action of Private ... in taking the departmental vehicle was entirely unauthorized.
Therefore they did not do anything at all about the matter and no redress is given to the person whose car was damaged. I do not think that is right. The army, the navy or the air force should be responsible if it is their vehicle which was responsible for the accident.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that the army is in the same position as any other employer. If an employee of a civilian firm takes his employer's automobile and goes out on a joy ride, and it is not for the purpose of the work for which he is employed, the employer is not responsible. Vicarious responsibility extends only if the employee is in the performance of the work for which he is employed. There is no difference there between the army or any other employer.
These accidents have happened in working hours, because these people have taken their vehicles out when they are supposed to be on duty.

With regard to the matter of the signal corps in the northwest territories, which was mentioned a few moments ago, I wish to refer particularly to some lads

who are stationed at Yellowknife. I understand that they have been there for over a year. I would urge the minister to draw that fact to the attention of the proper authorities and that these boys should have some leave. Some of them are married men and have not seen their wives for over a year. We are not now in a war period and these men should get some leave. How many men of the signal corps are in Whitehorse, Dawson City and Yellowknife?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to get that information and give it to my honourable friend a little later. With regard to the other point he mentioned, I shall take note of his remarks. We have had two or three cases of compassionate releases of personnel of the army stationed at Yellowknife.
I am not asking for release.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Leave. I shall look into the question. I imagine that some of them are highly skilled men and difficult to release.
I should like to refer to the matter of selection officers. The minister said selection was made by a personnel selection board.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is called a committee.
Can the minister give the names of the officers who are on that board? I should be interested in knowing who they are.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can give the names, but it will take a minute or two to get them.

We have heard of the splendid part played by the artillery services in the peacetime army, but I wish to draw attention to what is happening to men who in the past joined the army with the intention of making it their career. In one case I have in mind the man spent years in the service and was within sixty-nine days of receiving his pension when he made application to be retained in the services. He joined the nonpermanent forces back in 1926. Then he entered the permanent force in 1935 and joined up for the active service forces in 1939. He fought throughout. He rose from the ranks to the position of captain. Up to October 8, 1946, his pensionable service would be fifteen years and 296 days. He made application to join the army with the intention of making it his career. There has never been a black mark against his record. In fact all his service all the way through has been such that it has been recognized in the form of promotions from the lowest rank to the posi-

Supply-National Defence
tion which he now holds as commissioned officer. In spite of his efforts to remain in the army, he has been told he does not come up to the standard of some assessment officers or some group of officers who make the assessment. He is definitely out and he has no redress. He has been doing his best to find out what his crime is or what the difficulty is. All he is told is that he did not come up to the assessment, but he does not know the particulars. An example of this kind certainly works to the detriment of those who would like to make the army their career. He feels that he has been discriminated against, because he has examples of other men with less service and much lower qualifications, and certainly without the experience that he has had, who have been retained in the permanent force. It is utterly impossible for him to get any information. I suggest to the minister that, with that type of treatment, he is not going to get men to make the army their career, and this is Ac type of men who are needed.	"

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
give me the particulars of the case I shall look into it personally. We do not keep men in the service solely for the purpose of giving them a pension. At any rate we should not do so. There may be cases in which it is done. There may be some injustice in this case and I shall be glad to look into it.

I am not suggesting he is being cut off before his pension is due. I am sure the man does not want to remain in the army just to get his pension. I have already given the case to the minister, and his reply was that it has been handed over to a certain selection committee and that he has every confidence in it. And that is all there is to it. There is no redress for this man; he is just stuck. This is the kind of thing which does not reflect well on the officials of the army and which deters other good men from making the army a career, which it should be.

There are two other matters which I should like to bring up. First, I should like to bring to the attention of the committee sessional paper 153-G, dated April 23, 1946. The question dealt with pensions paid to retired members of the permanent armed forces. I do not bring this matter up for the purpose of criticizing the pensions, but to show how actuarially unsound the whole scheme of army pensions is. These figures are only up to the early part of April. From September 1, 1939, to April 1 of this year a total of 235 officers who had been non-commissioned officers in the ranks in the early days 63260-319J
of the war received pensions totalling $701,524.96. I imagine the figures are possibly double to-day. The reason I bring this up is that a non-commissioned officer as such pays nothing into the pension fund. Until they become officers there is no contribution. It is interesting to look down the list. One finds one sergeant-major, W.O.l, who retired with the rank of captain with a pension of $2,798.35 a year. Of the people included in this list, 115 are men who were in the ranks either as non-commissioned officers, warrant officers or privates in the early -days of the war, and therefore paid nothing into the fund. I notice there is one man who is a private and who paid nothing into the fund. The pension he receives to-day is $2,273.25. I wonder just how long the pension fund of the dominion government can stay sound under those circumstances. When the minister brings in his new bill I think some study should be given the whole pension act for the permanent force. Where a man gives service, we believe in a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We shall have first reading to-morrow morning of a bill in that regard.

The second point is in connection with the educational qualifications required of men joining the armed services to-day. I believe the hon. member for Nanaimo also mentioned that point. It occurs to me that if the minister desires a permanent force of 25,000 men, together with the surplus officers he expects, something will have to be done with regard to educational requirements, because I cannot see young men who have their senior matriculation joining the armed forces to spend the rest of their lives there I believe the minister should take men withi less than the high degree of education he appears to require to-day, and have a corps of schoolmasters such as they have in the British army to give these men part of their training along educational lines. It would be good for the men, and I am certain it would be good for the services. I would ask the minister whether any consideration has been given to the creation of a corps of schoolmasters to teach these men, so that while in the service their education may be brought up to a certain level.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: On the last question, we are continuing the educational service in the army to try to bring up the educational level of those who join the forces.

Pardon me; in other words, you are reducing the requirements?
Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No, not yet; but we are taking in a good many men, in several specialized corps, who perhaps do not have the minimum requirements we would like.
As to the question of pensioning non-commissioned officers, they had a statutory right to that pension, and we would be committing a breach of faith with them if, assuming they were no longer required in the army, we did not retire them on the pension to which they were entitled by law. In that respect we have paid the penalty, perhaps, for having such a small army before the war, because we were obliged to promote men to commissioned rank in order to use them as instructors and otherwise, who were not capable of holding those commissions in our post-war army. Briefly that is the explanation in that regard.
The hon. member for Calgary East asked the names of the members of the selection board. They are Brigadier Graham, deputy adjutant general of administration; Brigadier Gibson, Colonel Fleury, Lieutenant-Colonel Cherrier, and in each case a representative of the corps to which the officer applicant belongs. If he is a member of the infantry corps, there would be a representative of that corps, or the artillery corps, and so on.

There is just one further question I should like to ask the minister. When the Canadian government started recruiting for the Pacific campaign they set out certain advanced rates of pay for those who volunteered for Pacific service. Later certain personnel of the air force and those of H.M.C.S. Uganda were granted Pacific rates of pay, though the personnel of the Uganda did not volunteer for Pacific service. I am referring particularly to some three hundred army personnel who served in Australia and certain actual theatres of war, of whom about eighty or a hundred were radar personnel, radar mechanics. Has the department definitely decided what it is going to do with these men? Are they to receive Pacific rates of pay? They did not on demobilization, but will they be granted those rates?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think the answer is that they will not; they were not part of the Pacific force. That matter was considered over some period of time; I think it came up on my estimates last year, and the decision was that they would not receive Pacific rates of pay.

Some are receiving those rights who did not volunteer for Pacific service, while on the other hand those who were expecting to fight in the Pacific war, just because they were a month or two ahead are being deprived of this special rate.
I wonder if the minister is in a position now to answer my question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot answer that to-day. I have made inquiries, and the only information I have is that the officer referred to, Major Elliott, is no longer in the service. I shall give my hon. friend whatever information we have, either on my own estimates if they should not be concluded this evening, as I would hope they would be, or I am sure it would be in order for me to do so when the estimates of national defence for air are being considered. I shall have to get the information in the morning; we do not have it here.

There is another matter with which I should like to deal at this time; I do not think it has been dealt with as yet. It has to do with the men in the armed forces who committed military offences and were sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment, ^brought this question up last fall. I am not now dealing with offences which would be offences under the civil law; I am referring particularly to offences under military law. Last fall I brought up the question of the setting up of a judicial or semi-judicial board, and the minister advised that a board had been set up under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Keiller Mackay, with two distinguished co-members. That committee sat for a period of time reviewing sentences, and then I understand their work was discontinued. My question is, what is being done in reference to these prisoners who to-day are in gaols and penitentiaries, in regard to a further review of their sentences?
At the moment I have in mind particularly a man from the province of Saskatchewan. I am not going to give his name, though I shall give it to the minister privately, but his number was L-36119. He is of German parentage. He served overseas for two years. In the district whence he came there were several who found their way into an internment camp following their disloyal conduct at the beginning of the war. This man served throughout the Italian campaign, and later throughout the campaign in France and Germany. He had a fine record; he became a sergeant and then went over to England en route to Canada. There he became involved in the riots at Aldershot and received a sentence of three years' imprisonment. The provincial command of the Canadian Legion in Saskatchewan interested itself in this man, because while at the end of the war those who had been disloyal returned home from the internment camps, these men who served and

Supply-National Defence
who received very long sentences remained in prison. As a matter of fact I read over the evidence; and while in connection with military offences sentences are generally longer than they would be for civil offences of a like nature, I want to say that no counsel reading that evidence could but conclude that a maximum of three months would have been the normal sentence in a civil court. The provincial branch of the legion in Saskatchewan reviewed the matter and came to the same conclusion; and they came to the further conclusion that what he did at the time, impeding an officer, was the result of his nervous condition following service. It is the considered opinion of the provincial command that in his case the ends of justice would be met-and other cases are also mentioned- without any further imprisonment being exacted. I suggest this, that the time has now come for further review of those sentences imposed for purely military offences. I should like to ascertain from the minister how many soldiers who served overseas are to-day imprisoned, first in penitentiaries and, second, in the common gaols. In how many cases were sentences reviewed, and how many pardons granted, or reductions or diminutions in sentences passed by the court martial allowed? And a further question, in review, as to what further action will be taken in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not believe I can give the information exactly in the form requested. As at August 14 the total number of soldiers serving sentences and detention in Canada was 981. Of this total, about fifteen per cent, or 151, was for offences other than desertion or absenteeism, which would leave, roughly, 830 serving detentions for desertion or absenteeism.
The total number reviewed by the court martial board of review, which was presided over by Mr. Justice Mackay, was 1,895. Of those 1,895, those in which immediate release was recommended numbered 574; those where release was recommended at a future date, for remission of sentence, numbered 1,156, and those in which no recommendation for remission was made numbered 165. The cases of those still in detention are still under constant review by district officers commanding as well as by the adjutant general's department here in Ottawa.
Particularly in view of the announcement I made a day or so ago, it is my intention that a further complete review of all those ceases is to be made. I think the committee can be assured that clemency will be exercised in cases where it is considered appropriate. I
shall look into the particular case to which my hon. friend has .referred. He has given me the number, and I shall look into it personally.
I have a question to ask respecting pensions for the permanent force. When shall I have an opportunity to ask it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am bringing in a bill to-morrow to amend the Militia Pension Act. It will be given first reading, I would expect, and that would be an excellent opportunity for my hon. friend to raise the question.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but I have beep reading Hansard and I wish to make a correction. When the committee resumed its duties at eight o'clock I drew the attention of the minister to his policy respecting permanent force bands. I understood him to say that certain units would continue to have permanent force bands. Hansard so far-and I do not think the minister has had an opportunity to read it-does not reveal that. I thought the minister said that Canadian Ordnance Corps headquarters would continue to have a band.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did not say headquarters. I said there would be bands for such corps units as the Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps and the Royal Canadian Army Service Corps.

Having heard the names of the members of this selection board, I should like to say, first of all, that I could hardly disagree more strongly with them or with what they have done, than I do. I would strongly recommend to the minister that he call the members of this board together and have a talk with them over the matter of the selection of officers, to see if they cannot devise some type of selection system which will put into our army more officers who have had some experience and fewer who spent the war in passing red tape over desks-which is apparently what is happening.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Probably we should appoint the hon. member as sole member of the board.
You might do worse.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: You are too modest.

I will say that I was extremely glad to see Brigadier Graham's name on the list. I presume his presence there is what has caused as many as 1,140 men who did see fighting to be appointed. It is too bad that all the members of the board have not had the same experience as he had.
Supply-National Defence

I should like to learn from the minister how recruiting from the permanent force is coming along. He told us that we have 2,027 officers. How many O.R.'s are there?-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: About 700 this last month.
What is the total?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The total to date, as of July 31, is 13,518 all ranks.
In this 2,027 the total you will have, or are there still more to be appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As I say, the total to date is 13,518 all ranks, of which officers are 2,613, and the total establishment of officers when we are up to strength will be something over
3,000.

I wonder if the minister could be a little more- accurate. When we were talking about this matter before I asked the number of officers who had now been accepted for the permanent army, and he gave me the figure of 2,027. Now he says it is more than 2,600.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The figure is for the interim force as of July. 31. We have not taken anyone into the permanent force as yet.
Is this figure of 2,027 the right one, or is it 2,600?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I say that 2,027 is the number accepted for the permanent force. The figure of 2,613 is the number who are in the interim force. Probably the difference is accounted for by some of the remainder being still under consideration.
I am glad to have that cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is eleven o'clock; eight hours is long enough.

Apparently there are something like 11,000 O.R.'s in the permanent army. I should like to know something about their distribution, because I have it on very good authority that, as short a time as two months ago, the only permanent force field regiment we have did not have enough O.R.'s to clean their guns. They had to hire civilian labour. Perhaps that is still the case. I do not know, but I should like to. I am wondering whether all these 11,000 men are distributed around the country in offices of one kind or another, and permanent force units have not enough men to do even the essential duties.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, with-3ut question put, pursuant to standing order.

Tuesday, August 20, 1946
